explanation: Subjunctive were is used to talk about unreal, hypothetical, or imaginary situations. It is common after if, wish, and as if / as though, especially in formal English. In this pattern, were can be used with I, he, she, and it when the meaning is not real, not true now, or only imagined. For example: If I were you, I would wait; I wish he were here; She talks as if she were famous. In everyday spoken English, many native speakers say was instead of were in some of these sentences, but for IELTS and formal writing, were is usually the safer choice when the meaning is unreal.
explanationVi: Mệnh đề giả định với were dùng để nói về tình huống không có thật, không chắc là thật, hoặc chỉ là tưởng tượng. Nó thường đứng sau if, wish, và as if / as though, đặc biệt trong văn viết trang trọng. Ở mẫu này, were có thể dùng với I, he, she, it khi ý nghĩa là “không có thật” chứ không phải quá khứ thật. Ví dụ: If I were you, I would wait; I wish he were here; She talks as if she were famous. Trong tiếng Anh nói hàng ngày, người bản ngữ đôi khi vẫn nói was, nhưng trong IELTS và văn viết trang trọng, were thường là lựa chọn an toàn hơn khi nói về điều không có thật.
formPatterns: If + subject + were + adjective/noun, subject + would + verb
Subject + verb + as if/as though + subject + were + complement
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường dễ dùng thì quá khứ đơn was cho mọi trường hợp vì trong tiếng Việt không có hình thức chia động từ để biểu thị giả định như were. Cần nhớ were ở đây không phải để chỉ thời gian quá khứ, mà để chỉ điều không có thật hoặc trái với thực tế.

title: Sequence of Tenses
summary: Keeping tense consistent across a complex sentence, a common Writing accuracy loss.

commonMistakes.right: She said that she was tired.
commonMistakes.why: After a past reporting verb like said, English normally shifts the tense back. Vietnamese often keeps the same tense pattern, so learners may write the present form instead.
commonMistakes.wrong: She said that she is tired.

commonMistakes.right: They told us that they had finished the report.
commonMistakes.why: In reported speech, a past reporting verb usually causes earlier actions to move back into the past perfect. Vietnamese often expresses this without a tense shift.
commonMistakes.wrong: They told us that they have finished the report.

commonMistakes.right: I knew that he had left before noon.
commonMistakes.why: When the main clause is past, the earlier event is usually expressed with past perfect. Using simple past can make the time order unclear.
commonMistakes.wrong: I knew that he left before noon.

commonMistakes.right: If I were you, I would call her now.
commonMistakes.why: This is a hypothetical present situation, so English uses were in the if-clause and would in the main clause. Vietnamese learners often keep a simple present form in both parts.
commonMistakes.wrong: If I was you, I would call her now.

acceptedAnswers: She said that she was tired.
choices: She said that she is tired.
She said that she was tired.
She said that she has tired.
drills.explanation: After the past reporting verb said, the present tense usually shifts back to the past tense in reported speech.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She said that she was tired.

acceptedAnswers: They told us that they had finished the report.
drills.explanation: The reporting verb told is past, and the earlier action finishes before that past moment, so past perfect is needed.
drills.prompt: Write the sentence in correct reported speech: They / tell / us / finish / the report
drills.target: They told us that they had finished the report.

acceptedAnswers: I knew that he had left before noon.
drills.explanation: The knowing happened in the past, and the leaving happened earlier, so English uses past perfect for the earlier event.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence in correct tense sequence: I knew. He left before noon.
drills.target: I knew that he had left before noon.

acceptedAnswers: If I were you, I would call her now.
choices: If I was you, I would call her now.
If I were you, I would call her now.
If I am you, I will call her now.
drills.explanation: For a hypothetical present situation, English uses were in the if-clause and would in the main clause.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: If I were you, I would call her now.

acceptedAnswers: He said that he would call me later.
drills.explanation: Would is the usual backshift of will in reported speech after a past reporting verb.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: He said that he will call me later.
drills.target: He said that he would call me later.

acceptedAnswers: By the time we arrived, the meeting had started.
drills.explanation: The meeting started before our arrival, so past perfect shows the earlier past event clearly.
drills.prompt: Use these words to make a correct sentence: by the time / we / arrive / the meeting / start
drills.target: By the time we arrived, the meeting had started.

acceptedAnswers: She promised that she would help me the next day.
choices: She promised that she will help me the next day.
She promised that she would help me the next day.
She promised that she helps me the next day.
drills.explanation: After the past verb promised, the future idea is normally backshifted to would.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She promised that she would help me the next day.

acceptedAnswers: I thought that the train was delayed.
drills.explanation: The thinking is in the past, so the earlier state is usually reported with a past form.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: I thought that the train is delayed.
drills.target: I thought that the train was delayed.

acceptedAnswers: She said that she had lost her keys.
drills.explanation: The loss happened before she spoke, so past perfect is the normal sequence of tenses here.
drills.prompt: Write the correct reported sentence: she said / lose / her keys
drills.target: She said that she had lost her keys.

acceptedAnswers: When I got home, my brother had already gone to bed.
choices: When I got home, my brother already went to bed.
When I got home, my brother had already gone to bed.
When I got home, my brother has already gone to bed.
drills.explanation: The going to bed happened before the moment I got home, so past perfect is needed.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: When I got home, my brother had already gone to bed.

acceptedAnswers: The teacher explained that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
drills.explanation: Scientific facts usually keep the present tense even inside a past reporting sentence, because they are still true.
drills.prompt: Rewrite correctly: The teacher explained that water boil at 100 degrees Celsius.
drills.target: The teacher explained that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.

acceptedAnswers: He asked whether I had seen his email.
choices: He asked whether I saw his email.
He asked whether I had seen his email.
He asked whether I have seen his email.
drills.explanation: The asking is in the past, and the seeing happened before that, so past perfect is the safest sequence.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He asked whether I had seen his email.

explanation: Sequence of tenses means matching verb tense to the time relationships inside a sentence, especially in reported speech and complex sentences. When the reporting verb is past, English often shifts the following tense back: present becomes past, will becomes would, and an earlier event often becomes past perfect. This helps show which action happened first, and it is one of the most common accuracy problems for Vietnamese learners because Vietnamese often does not require the same tense shift. Some clauses do not shift, especially when they state general truths, scientific facts, or things still true now.
explanationVi: Sequence of tenses là cách phối hợp thì trong một câu phức để người đọc hiểu rõ sự việc nào xảy ra trước, sự việc nào xảy ra sau. Điểm này rất quan trọng trong câu tường thuật và các mệnh đề phụ. Khi động từ tường thuật ở quá khứ, tiếng Anh thường lùi thì ở mệnh đề sau: hiện tại thường lùi về quá khứ, will lùi về would, và một hành động xảy ra sớm hơn thường dùng quá khứ hoàn thành. Ví dụ: She said that she was tired; They told us that they had finished the report; I knew that he had left before noon. Đây là lỗi rất hay gặp với người Việt vì tiếng Việt không bắt buộc phải đổi thì theo kiểu này. Nhiều khi người học dùng nguyên thì hiện tại sau said/told/knew, nhưng trong tiếng Anh như vậy thường sai khi đang kể lại lời nói hay suy nghĩ ở quá khứ. Tuy nhiên, không phải lúc nào cũng lùi thì. Các chân lý chung, sự thật khoa học, hoặc điều vẫn đúng ở hiện tại thường giữ thì hiện tại: The teacher explained that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. Với câu điều kiện không thật ở hiện tại, tiếng Anh dùng were trong mệnh đề if và would ở mệnh đề chính: If I were you, I would call her now. Cần chú ý rằng việc lùi thì không chỉ là “đổi quá khứ cho có”, mà là cách đánh dấu quan hệ thời gian và mức độ xa của sự việc trong câu.
formPatterns: past reporting verb + backshift in reported clause
general truth and scientific fact often keep present tense
hypothetical present condition: if + were, would + base verb
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không lùi thì mạnh như tiếng Anh trong câu tường thuật, nên người học dễ viết giữ nguyên thì hiện tại sau said/told/knew hoặc quên đổi will thành would. Cũng dễ nhầm giữa past simple và past perfect vì tiếng Việt hay dựa vào từ chỉ thời gian hơn là hình thái động từ.

title: Can for Ability
summary: Present ability and permission with can.

commonMistakes.right: I can swim.
commonMistakes.why: Use can + base verb to show ability.
commonMistakes.wrong: I can to swim.

commonMistakes.right: She can speak English.
commonMistakes.why: Do not add -s to can. The main verb after can stays in the base form.
commonMistakes.wrong: She cans speak English.

commonMistakes.right: Can you help me?
commonMistakes.why: In questions, can comes before the subject.
commonMistakes.wrong: You can help me?

commonMistakes.right: We can go now.
commonMistakes.why: After can, use the base form of the verb, not the -ing form.
commonMistakes.wrong: We can going now.

acceptedAnswers: I can ride a bike.
choices: I can ride a bike.
I can to ride a bike.
I cans ride a bike.
drills.explanation: Can shows ability, and the verb after can is in the base form.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I can ride a bike.

acceptedAnswers: Can you speak English?
choices: You can speak English?
Can you speak English?
Do you can speak English?
drills.explanation: In questions, can comes before the subject.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct question.
drills.target: Can you speak English?

acceptedAnswers: She can run very fast.
drills.explanation: Can is followed by the base form of the verb.
drills.prompt: Use these words to make a sentence: She / can / run / very fast.
drills.target: She can run very fast.

acceptedAnswers: can
drills.explanation: The correct question form is Can you ...?
drills.prompt: ____ you help me?
drills.target: can

acceptedAnswers: He can play the piano.
drills.explanation: This sentence shows ability. After can, use the base form play.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with can: He is able to play the piano.
drills.target: He can play the piano.

acceptedAnswers: I can cook dinner.
drills.explanation: Can + base verb is the correct structure for ability.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: I can to cook dinner.
drills.target: I can cook dinner.

acceptedAnswers: They can hear the music.
choices: They can hear the music.
They can hearing the music.
They cans hear the music.
drills.explanation: Only the base form hear is correct after can.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: They can hear the music.

acceptedAnswers: We can start now.
drills.explanation: This is a correct sentence showing present ability or possibility.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence about ability using can and start.
drills.target: We can start now.

acceptedAnswers: can
drills.explanation: Can is the correct modal for ability here.
drills.prompt: I ____ speak Vietnamese and English.
drills.target: can

explanation: Can is a modal verb used for present ability and permission. Use can + base verb: I can swim, she can help, they can go. In questions, put can before the subject: Can you come? Do not add -s to can, and do not use to after it.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt hay thêm to sau can hoặc dùng sai trật tự câu hỏi như tiếng Việt. Cũng dễ thêm -s vào can trong câu với she/he.

title: Cannot for Inability
summary: Negative ability and prohibition with cannot.

commonMistakes.right: I cannot swim.
commonMistakes.why: Use cannot to say you do not have the ability to do something.
commonMistakes.wrong: I do not can swim.

commonMistakes.right: She cannot open the door.
commonMistakes.why: Cannot is the correct negative form of can for inability.
commonMistakes.wrong: She does not can open the door.

commonMistakes.right: We cannot see the mountain from here.
commonMistakes.why: Use cannot + base verb to show inability or lack of possibility.
commonMistakes.wrong: We cannot sees the mountain from here.

commonMistakes.right: He cannot come to the party tonight.
commonMistakes.why: Cannot is also used for something that is not possible or not allowed.
commonMistakes.wrong: He can not comes to the party tonight.

acceptedAnswers: cannot
drills.explanation: Use cannot to make can negative.
drills.prompt: I ____ swim.
drills.target: cannot

acceptedAnswers: cannot
drills.explanation: Cannot is the negative form used for inability.
drills.prompt: She ____ drive a car.
drills.target: cannot

acceptedAnswers: I cannot sing.
choices: I do not can sing.
I cannot sing.
I cannot sings.
drills.explanation: The correct negative form is cannot + base verb.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I cannot sing.

acceptedAnswers: They cannot hear us.
choices: They do not can hear us.
They cannot hear us.
They cannot hears us.
drills.explanation: Cannot is followed by the base verb hear.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: They cannot hear us.

acceptedAnswers: I cannot open this box.
drills.explanation: Write cannot before the base verb open.
drills.prompt: Write the sentence: I / cannot / open / this box.
drills.target: I cannot open this box.

acceptedAnswers: She cannot play the piano.
drills.explanation: Cannot shows that she has no ability to play the piano.
drills.prompt: Rewrite in the negative: She can play the piano.
drills.target: She cannot play the piano.

acceptedAnswers: We cannot go now.
drills.explanation: Cannot is used here to show that going now is not possible.
drills.prompt: We do not can go now.
drills.target: We cannot go now.

acceptedAnswers: He cannot cook.
choices: He cannot cooks.
He cannot cook.
He does not can cook.
drills.explanation: Cannot must be followed by the base verb cook.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He cannot cook.

acceptedAnswers: cannot
drills.explanation: Cannot is the negative form of can in this sentence.
drills.prompt: We ____ speak English.
drills.target: cannot

explanation: Use cannot to say that someone has no ability to do something, or that something is not possible or not allowed. It is followed by the base verb: cannot swim, cannot go, cannot open. In spoken English, people often say can't, which means the same thing.
formPatterns: cannot is followed by a bare infinitive
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường dùng cấu trúc phủ định với do not/does not + can, nhưng tiếng Anh chuẩn là cannot/can't + động từ nguyên mẫu không to.

title: Could for Past Ability
summary: General past ability, and why it is not used for one completed achievement.

commonMistakes.right: I could swim when I was five.
commonMistakes.why: Could is used for general ability in the past.
commonMistakes.wrong: I was able to swim when I was five.

commonMistakes.right: She could speak French very well as a child.
commonMistakes.why: Could is correct for a past ability that lasted over time.
commonMistakes.wrong: She can speak French very well as a child.

commonMistakes.right: I could not find my keys this morning.
commonMistakes.why: Could not expresses past inability.
commonMistakes.wrong: I could find my keys this morning.

commonMistakes.right: He could play the piano when he was young.
commonMistakes.why: Could shows a general past skill or ability.
commonMistakes.wrong: He can play the piano when he was young.

acceptedAnswers: could
drills.explanation: Could is the modal used here to talk about ability in the past.
drills.prompt: I _____ ride a bike when I was six.
drills.target: could

acceptedAnswers: She could speak English when she was a child.
drills.explanation: Could is correct because the sentence describes a general past ability.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence about a past ability: she / speak English / when she was a child.
drills.target: She could speak English when she was a child.

acceptedAnswers: I could not run very fast when I was younger.
drills.explanation: Could not is the normal way to say there was no ability in the past.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence to show past inability: I cannot run very fast now, but I was younger.
drills.target: I could not run very fast when I was younger.

acceptedAnswers: Could she read when she was four?
drills.explanation: Could is used in questions about past ability.
drills.prompt: Make a question: she / read / when she was four
drills.target: Could she read when she was four?

acceptedAnswers: I could not finish the race because I was injured.
drills.explanation: Could is correct because the sentence talks about a past lack of ability.
drills.prompt: I can not finish the race because I was injured.
drills.target: I could not finish the race because I was injured.

acceptedAnswers: Could you dance when you were a teenager?
choices: Can you dance when you were a teenager?
Could you dance when you were a teenager?
Could you danced when you were a teenager?
drills.explanation: Could is the correct past form. Can is present time, and danced is not correct after could.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Could you dance when you were a teenager?

acceptedAnswers: He could speak three languages before he went to university.
drills.explanation: Could is used for a general ability before another past time.
drills.prompt: Rewrite using could: He was able to speak three languages before he went to university.
drills.target: He could speak three languages before he went to university.

acceptedAnswers: could not
drills.explanation: Could not shows past inability.
drills.prompt: I _____ remember her name yesterday.
drills.target: could not

acceptedAnswers: She could understand the instructions.
choices: She could understands the instructions.
She can understand the instructions.
She could understand the instructions.
drills.explanation: Could is correct for past ability. Can changes the time to the present, and understands is wrong after could.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She could understand the instructions.

explanation: Could is used to talk about general ability in the past. It often describes a skill, a repeated ability, or something someone was able to do over a period of time: I could swim when I was a child. It is not the normal choice for one finished achievement at a single moment. For that, English often uses was able to, managed to, or a different past-tense verb: I managed to open the door after several tries.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường chỉ cần một động từ quá khứ hoặc 'có thể' cho cả khả năng chung và một lần làm được việc gì đó, nên người học dễ dùng 'could' cho mọi trường hợp quá khứ. Trong tiếng Anh, 'could' thường nói về khả năng chung trong quá khứ, không phải một thành công duy nhất.

title: Must for Obligation
summary: Strong internal obligation.

commonMistakes.right: You must wear a helmet when you ride a motorcycle.
commonMistakes.why: must shows a strong rule or obligation.
commonMistakes.wrong: You have to wearing a helmet when you ride a motorcycle.

commonMistakes.right: Students must not use their phones during the exam.
commonMistakes.why: must not is the negative form for a strict prohibition.
commonMistakes.wrong: Students mustn't to use their phones during the exam.

commonMistakes.right: I must finish this report tonight.
commonMistakes.why: must is followed by the base form of the verb, not an infinitive with to.
commonMistakes.wrong: I must to finish this report tonight.

commonMistakes.right: We must be quiet in the library.
commonMistakes.why: after must, the verb stays in the base form: be, not am/is/are or being.
commonMistakes.wrong: We must are quiet in the library.

acceptedAnswers: must
drills.explanation: must expresses a strong obligation or necessity.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: You ___ wear a seatbelt in the car.
drills.target: must

acceptedAnswers: must not
choices: must not
do not must
must to not
drills.explanation: must not is the correct negative form for prohibition.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: must not

acceptedAnswers: I must call my mother tonight.
drills.explanation: The sentence uses must + base verb to show obligation.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with must: call / mother / tonight
drills.target: I must call my mother tonight.

acceptedAnswers: You must arrive early.
You must be early.
drills.explanation: Both sentences are correct. must is followed by the base form of the verb.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using must: It is necessary for you to arrive early.
drills.target: You must arrive early.

acceptedAnswers: must
drills.explanation: must is the modal used for strong obligation.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: We ___ submit the form today.
drills.target: must

acceptedAnswers: You must be quiet in class.
drills.explanation: must + base verb be is correct. The verb after must does not change to are or is.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: You must are quiet in class.
drills.target: You must be quiet in class.

acceptedAnswers: must
drills.explanation: must is used to show a rule, duty, or strong necessity.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I ___ finish this assignment before I go out.
drills.target: must

acceptedAnswers: You must not smoke here.
drills.explanation: must not is the correct form for a strong prohibition.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: You mustn't to smoke here.
drills.target: You must not smoke here.

acceptedAnswers: You must bring your passport.
You must bring a passport.
drills.explanation: must + base verb is the correct pattern. The object can be specific or general depending on meaning.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using must: It is necessary for you to bring your passport.
drills.target: You must bring your passport.

explanation: Must for obligation expresses a strong rule, duty, or necessity. In this pattern, must is followed by the base form of the verb: must go, must be, must finish. The negative form must not shows prohibition.
l1Notes: Người học Việt thường thêm to sau must, như “must to do”, hoặc dùng have to thay cho must trong mọi trường hợp. Cũng dễ nhầm must not với cấu trúc phủ định khác trong tiếng Việt, nên cần nhớ must not + động từ nguyên mẫu.

title: Have To for Obligation
summary: External obligation, and the only form available in past and future.

commonMistakes.right: I have to wear a uniform at work.
commonMistakes.why: have to is the normal form for an obligation that comes from rules, an employer, a law, or a situation.
commonMistakes.wrong: I must to wear a uniform at work.

commonMistakes.right: She had to leave early because of the storm.
commonMistakes.why: In the past, obligation is normally expressed with had to, not must.
commonMistakes.wrong: She must leave early because of the storm.

commonMistakes.right: We will have to pay for the tickets tomorrow.
commonMistakes.why: For future obligation, English uses will have to. Must is not the normal future form.
commonMistakes.wrong: We must pay for the tickets tomorrow.

commonMistakes.right: Do you have to work on Saturday?
commonMistakes.why: Questions with have to are formed with do/does/did. You do not say have you to in modern English.
commonMistakes.wrong: Have you to work on Saturday?

acceptedAnswers: I have to get up at 6 a.m.
choices: I have to get up at 6 a.m.
I must to get up at 6 a.m.
I have got to get up at 6 a.m.
drills.explanation: have to is correct for obligation here. must to is wrong, and have got to is a different spoken form that is not the focus of this lesson.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I have to get up at 6 a.m.

acceptedAnswers: has to
drills.explanation: Use has to with he, she, or it in the present simple.
drills.prompt: She ___ finish the report today.
drills.target: has to

acceptedAnswers: I had to call the doctor yesterday.
drills.explanation: In the past, the correct form is had to. Must does not normally replace it.
drills.prompt: Write a full sentence. Use: I / had to / call the doctor / yesterday
drills.target: I had to call the doctor yesterday.

acceptedAnswers: We will have to leave early tomorrow.
drills.explanation: For future obligation, English uses will have to.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence in the future: We have to leave early tomorrow.
drills.target: We will have to leave early tomorrow.

acceptedAnswers: Do you have to wear a tie at school?
choices: Do you have to wear a tie at school?
Have you to wear a tie at school?
Do you must wear a tie at school?
drills.explanation: Questions with have to use do/does/did. Have you to is not standard modern English.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct question.
drills.target: Do you have to wear a tie at school?

acceptedAnswers: must
drills.explanation: must shows strong obligation, often from the speaker. This lesson contrasts it with have to, which usually means external obligation.
drills.prompt: I ___ finish this now because my manager told me to.
drills.target: must

acceptedAnswers: They have to pay the bill before they leave.
drills.explanation: have to is correct for an outside obligation, such as a rule or requirement.
drills.prompt: Write a full sentence. Use: They / have to / pay the bill / before they leave
drills.target: They have to pay the bill before they leave.

acceptedAnswers: Does your brother have to work on Sunday?
drills.explanation: In questions, use does with he, she, or it, then have to.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: Does your brother has to work on Sunday?
drills.target: Does your brother have to work on Sunday?

acceptedAnswers: You have to show your passport at the airport.
choices: You have to show your passport at the airport.
You must to show your passport at the airport.
You have show your passport at the airport.
drills.explanation: have to is the correct form for an external requirement such as airport control. The other options are ungrammatical.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: You have to show your passport at the airport.

acceptedAnswers: I do not have to go today.
drills.explanation: Negative have to means there is no obligation. Do not use must not, because that means prohibition.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence as a negative: I have to go today.
drills.target: I do not have to go today.

explanation:
Have to is used for obligation, especially when the obligation comes from outside the speaker: rules, laws, schedules, employers, or other people. In the present simple, it changes like a normal verb: I/you/we/they have to, he/she/it has to. In questions and negatives, it uses do/does/did: Do you have to...?, I do not have to....

For past obligation, English normally uses had to. For future obligation, English normally uses will have to. That is why have to is especially useful: it covers present, past, and future more naturally than must.

Compare it with must: must often means the speaker feels the obligation is strong or necessary. In everyday English, have to is more common for rules and outside requirements, while must is less common and more formal in many contexts.
formPatterns: do not/does not/did not have to + base verb
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng phải cho cả nghĩa ép buộc từ bên ngoài lẫn nghĩa bắt buộc nói chung, nên người học dễ dùng must thay cho have to trong mọi ngữ cảnh. Cần lưu ý have to thường hợp với quy định, lịch trình, và yêu cầu từ người khác; quá khứ là had to, tương lai là will have to.

minimalPairs.meaning: Strong internal obligation or speaker-determined necessity.
minimalPairs.sentence: I must finish this today.

minimalPairs.meaning: External obligation from a rule, schedule, or other person.
minimalPairs.sentence: I have to finish this today.

title: Must Not vs Do Not Have To
summary: Prohibition versus absence of obligation, a meaning reversal learners routinely miss.

commonMistakes.right: You must not smoke here.
commonMistakes.why: Must not means prohibition. It says something is not allowed.
commonMistakes.wrong: You do not have to smoke here.

commonMistakes.right: You do not have to come to the meeting.
commonMistakes.why: Do not have to means there is no obligation. It says something is optional, not forbidden.
commonMistakes.wrong: You must not come to the meeting.

commonMistakes.right: Students must not use phones during the exam.
commonMistakes.why: Must not is used for rules and bans.
commonMistakes.wrong: Students do not have to use phones during the exam.

commonMistakes.right: You do not have to pay now.
commonMistakes.why: Do not have to means payment is optional or delayed; it does not mean paying is forbidden.
commonMistakes.wrong: You must not pay now.

drills.explanation: Must not shows prohibition or strong ban. It is the opposite of permission, not the same as no obligation.

acceptedAnswers: must not
choices: must not
do not have to
have to
drills.explanation: Must not expresses a rule or ban. Do not have to means optional, so it does not fit here.

drills.prompt: Choose the sentence that means the action is forbidden.

drills.target: You do not have to bring any food.

explanation: Must not and do not have to are very different in meaning. Must not means prohibition: something is not allowed. Do not have to means no obligation: something is optional, not required. This difference is very important for IELTS because Vietnamese learners often translate both ideas with one structure like ‘không phải’ or ‘không cần’, but in English the meaning changes completely depending on the modal. Compare it with must for obligation and have to for obligation: must and have to both express necessity or requirement, while must not expresses a ban and do not have to expresses freedom from obligation.
explanationVi: ‘Must not’ và ‘do not have to’ khác nhau hoàn toàn về nghĩa. ‘Must not’ diễn tả cấm đoán, nghĩa là một hành động không được phép làm. Còn ‘do not have to’ diễn tả không có nghĩa vụ, tức là không bắt buộc phải làm, nhưng vẫn có thể làm nếu muốn. Đây là điểm rất dễ nhầm với người Việt vì trong tiếng Việt đều có thể được hiểu gần như ‘không được’ hoặc ‘không cần’, nhưng trong tiếng Anh hai cấu trúc này không thay thế cho nhau. Hãy nhớ: ‘must not’ = cấm; ‘do not have to’ = không bắt buộc. Ngoài ra, ‘must’ và ‘have to’ đều dùng cho nghĩa bắt buộc/nghĩa vụ, còn ‘must not’ là cấm và ‘do not have to’ là không bắt buộc.

do not have to = no obligation

title: Modals of Deduction (Past)
summary: Must have, might have, and cannot have for conclusions about the past.

commonMistakes.right: She must have missed the train because she is late.
commonMistakes.why: Use must have + past participle to make a strong deduction about a finished past event.
commonMistakes.wrong: She must miss the train because she is late.

commonMistakes.right: He might have forgotten his keys, so he cannot get into the house.
commonMistakes.why: Use might have + past participle for a possible past reason, and cannot have + past participle for a past conclusion that is impossible or very unlikely.
commonMistakes.wrong: He might forget his keys, so he cannot get into the house.

commonMistakes.right: They cannot have left yet because their car is still outside.
commonMistakes.why: Cannot have + past participle is used to say a past event was impossible or highly unlikely. The base form cannot express this past deduction.
commonMistakes.wrong: They cannot leave yet because their car is still outside.

commonMistakes.right: I think she must have been tired after the long flight.
commonMistakes.why: After must have, use a past participle. Be careful not to use an adjective or base verb after must have.
commonMistakes.wrong: I think she must have tired after the long flight.

acceptedAnswers: must have
drills.explanation: Use must have + past participle to make a strong deduction about the past.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: She ______ forgotten her passport.

drills.explanation: Use cannot have + past participle to say a past event was impossible or very unlikely.

acceptedAnswers: might have
drills.explanation: Use might have + past participle for a possible past cause or event.

drills.explanation: Cannot have + past participle is the correct form for a deduction about the past. The other options use the wrong verb form or the wrong time.

explanation:
Modals of deduction in the past are used to guess or conclude what happened earlier. The structure is modal + have + past participle: must have for a strong conclusion, might have for a possible conclusion, and cannot have for a conclusion that something was impossible or very unlikely.

After have, English needs the past participle, not the base verb. So you say must have gone, might have lost, and cannot have finished. These forms are about a finished past event, not the present.

Use must have when the evidence is strong: She must have missed the train. Use might have when you are unsure: She might have missed the train. Use cannot have when the conclusion is negative and strong: She cannot have missed the train because she is already here.

A common Vietnamese error is to use the base verb after must/might/cannot, or to translate directly as “must” without the extra have. In English, the past meaning must be shown with have + past participle.
explanationVi:
Trong tiếng Anh, khi đoán về một sự việc đã xảy ra trong quá khứ, ta thường dùng cấu trúc: modal + have + past participle (động từ ở dạng quá khứ phân từ). Ví dụ: must have gone, might have lost, cannot have finished.

Must have dùng khi người nói gần như chắc chắn về một kết luận trong quá khứ, dựa vào dấu hiệu hoặc bằng chứng: She must have missed the train. = Chắc là cô ấy đã lỡ tàu. Might have dùng khi chỉ là khả năng, chưa chắc chắn: She might have missed the train. = Có lẽ cô ấy đã lỡ tàu. Cannot have dùng khi kết luận rằng việc đó không thể xảy ra hoặc rất khó xảy ra: She cannot have missed the train because she is already here. = Cô ấy không thể đã lỡ tàu vì cô ấy đã ở đây rồi.

Điểm rất quan trọng là sau have phải dùng past participle, không dùng động từ nguyên mẫu. Vì vậy không nói must miss, might lose, cannot finish để diễn tả phán đoán về quá khứ. Cũng không bỏ have trong các cấu trúc này. Trong IELTS, lỗi phổ biến của người học Việt là dịch trực tiếp từ tiếng Việt nên quên rằng tiếng Anh phải có have + V3 để nói về suy đoán quá khứ.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt hay thiếu have hoặc dùng động từ nguyên mẫu sau must/might/cannot vì trong tiếng Việt không có hình thái chia như vậy khi suy đoán về quá khứ.

title: Need Not Have
summary: An unnecessary action that was nonetheless performed.

commonMistakes.right: I needn't have bought bread because my sister had already bought some.
commonMistakes.why: Needn't have + past participle means the action was unnecessary, even though it happened.
commonMistakes.wrong: I didn't need to buy bread because my sister had already bought some.

commonMistakes.right: She needn't have stayed up so late because the meeting was cancelled.
commonMistakes.why: This form shows that staying up late was unnecessary after the action happened.
commonMistakes.wrong: She didn't need to stay up so late because the meeting was cancelled.

commonMistakes.right: They needn't have rushed to the station because the train was delayed.
commonMistakes.why: Needn't have is used when someone did something that later turned out to be unnecessary.
commonMistakes.wrong: They didn't need to rush to the station because the train was delayed.

commonMistakes.right: He needn't have called me three times; I was already on my way.
commonMistakes.why: Needn't have emphasizes that the calling happened, but it was not necessary.
commonMistakes.wrong: He didn't need to call me three times; I was already on my way.

acceptedAnswers: needn't have
drills.explanation: Use needn't have + past participle to say an action happened, but it was unnecessary.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: You __________ bought that umbrella; it stopped raining.
drills.target: needn't have

acceptedAnswers: I needn't have printed the tickets because the airline had already emailed them.
drills.explanation: This sentence is correct because it shows that printing the tickets was unnecessary, even though it happened.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence about printing the tickets. Say that the action was unnecessary, but it happened.
drills.target: I needn't have printed the tickets because the airline had already emailed them.

acceptedAnswers: She needn't have waited outside for an hour.
drills.explanation: Needn't have is followed by a past participle. The sentence means her waiting happened, but it was unnecessary.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence to show that the waiting was unnecessary, but it happened: She waited outside for an hour, but it was unnecessary.
drills.target: She needn't have waited outside for an hour.

acceptedAnswers: He needn't have bought a new charger because mine worked fine.
drills.explanation: The structure needn't have bought shows a completed action that turned out not to be necessary.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence using needn't have + past participle. Say that buying a new charger was unnecessary.
drills.target: He needn't have bought a new charger because mine worked fine.

acceptedAnswers: I needn't have taken a taxi; the metro was faster.
drills.explanation: This is correct because taking a taxi was done, but it was not necessary in the end.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: I didn't need to take a taxi; the metro was faster.
drills.target: I needn't have taken a taxi; the metro was faster.

acceptedAnswers: She needn't have cooked dinner because her friends brought food.
choices: She didn't need to cook dinner because her friends brought food.
She needn't have cooked dinner because her friends brought food.
She needn't cooked dinner because her friends brought food.
drills.explanation: Needn't have + past participle is the form used when the cooking happened but was unnecessary. The other option with needn't cooked is ungrammatical.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She needn't have cooked dinner because her friends brought food.

acceptedAnswers: They needn't have booked a hotel for one night.
choices: They needn't have book a hotel for one night.
They needn't have booked a hotel for one night.
They didn't need to booked a hotel for one night.
drills.explanation: After needn't have, use the past participle booked. The other options are ungrammatical.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: They needn't have booked a hotel for one night.

acceptedAnswers: You needn't have brought your laptop to the meeting.
choices: You needn't have bring your laptop to the meeting.
You needn't have brought your laptop to the meeting.
You didn't need bringing your laptop to the meeting.
drills.explanation: The correct form is needn't have + past participle. Brought is the past participle of bring.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: You needn't have brought your laptop to the meeting.

acceptedAnswers: We needn't have left so early because the concert started late.
drills.explanation: This sentence shows that leaving early happened, but it was unnecessary because of the late start.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with needn't have about leaving early for a concert.
drills.target: We needn't have left so early because the concert started late.

explanation: Needn't have + past participle is used when someone did something, but later it turns out the action was unnecessary. The action still happened, so this form is different from didn't need to, which usually means the action was unnecessary and often implies it was not done. In IELTS writing and speaking, use needn't have when you want to show regret, wasted effort, or unnecessary action after the fact. The pattern is needn't have + past participle: needn't have gone, needn't have bought, needn't have waited.
explanationVi: Needn't have + V3/V-ed dùng khi một hành động ĐÃ xảy ra, nhưng sau đó mới biết là hành động đó không cần thiết. Nghĩa là người nói/người viết vẫn làm việc đó, nhưng việc làm ấy là “thừa”, “phí công”, hoặc “không đáng phải làm”. Ví dụ: I needn't have bought bread. = Tôi đã mua bánh mì, nhưng hóa ra không cần mua. Đây khác với didn't need to. Didn't need to thường nhấn mạnh là “không cần phải làm”, và rất hay dùng cho việc chưa làm hoặc không nhấn vào việc đã làm rồi. Trong IELTS, hãy nhớ: needn't have = đã làm rồi nhưng không cần; cấu trúc là needn't have + past participle: needn't have gone, needn't have called, needn't have waited.
l1Notes: Người Việt hay dùng “không cần phải” cho cả hai tình huống: việc không làm và việc đã làm rồi. Trong tiếng Anh phải phân biệt: needn't have nói về hành động đã xảy ra nhưng là thừa; didn't need to thường chỉ đơn giản là không cần làm, và có thể không ngụ ý rằng hành động đã diễn ra.

title: Would Rather
summary: Preference, including the past-form pattern after a change of subject.

commonMistakes.right: I would rather stay at home tonight.
commonMistakes.why: Would rather is followed by the base form of the verb when the subject stays the same.
commonMistakes.wrong: I would rather to stay at home tonight.

commonMistakes.right: She would rather not drive in the rain.
commonMistakes.why: Use would rather + base verb, and put not before the verb to make it negative.
commonMistakes.wrong: She would rather don't drive in the rain.

commonMistakes.right: I would rather you left now.
commonMistakes.why: After would rather with a different subject, English often uses a past form to express a present preference.
commonMistakes.wrong: I would rather you leave now.

commonMistakes.right: He would rather I had called earlier.
commonMistakes.why: When the preference refers to a past situation and the subject changes, English uses a past perfect form.
commonMistakes.wrong: He would rather I called earlier.

acceptedAnswers: stay
drills.explanation: After would rather, use the base form of the verb when the subject is the same.
drills.prompt: I would rather _____ at home tonight.
drills.target: stay

acceptedAnswers: I would rather not go out tonight.
choices: I would rather don't go out tonight.
I would rather not go out tonight.
I would rather not to go out tonight.
drills.explanation: Would rather takes the base verb, and not comes before it.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I would rather not go out tonight.

acceptedAnswers: I would rather you left now.
drills.explanation: With a different subject, would rather is often followed by a past form to express a present preference.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence: prefer that you leave now
drills.target: I would rather you left now.

acceptedAnswers: left
drills.explanation: After would rather with a different subject, the verb is often in the past form.
drills.prompt: She would rather I _____ early.
drills.target: left

acceptedAnswers: He would rather I had called earlier.
choices: He would rather I called earlier.
He would rather I had called earlier.
He would rather I have called earlier.
drills.explanation: For a past situation with a different subject, would rather often uses the past perfect.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He would rather I had called earlier.

acceptedAnswers: I would rather stay in tonight than go to a party.
drills.explanation: Would rather can be followed by one preference contrasted with another using than.
drills.prompt: Rewrite with would rather: I prefer staying in tonight to going to a party.
drills.target: I would rather stay in tonight than go to a party.

acceptedAnswers: leave
drills.explanation: The verb after would rather is the base form.
drills.prompt: They would rather we _____ early tomorrow.
drills.target: leave

acceptedAnswers: She would rather not answer the phone now.
choices: She would rather not answers the phone now.
She would rather not answer the phone now.
She would rather doesn't answer the phone now.
drills.explanation: Use the base verb after would rather, and place not before it.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She would rather not answer the phone now.

acceptedAnswers: I would rather you were honest with me.
drills.explanation: With a different subject, would rather is often followed by a past form such as were or were to express a present preference.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: I would rather you are honest with me.
drills.target: I would rather you were honest with me.

explanation: Would rather is used to express preference. With the same subject, it is followed by the base form: I would rather stay. With a different subject, English often uses a past form to express a present preference: I would rather you left. For a past preference with a different subject, English often uses the past perfect: I would rather you had called earlier. Not is placed before the verb: would rather not go.
l1Notes: Người học Việt thường muốn dùng động từ nguyên mẫu sau to hoặc thêm do/does/did theo kiểu tiếng Việt; cần nhớ would rather đi trực tiếp với động từ nguyên thể không to, và khi đổi chủ ngữ thì tiếng Anh dùng dạng quá khứ để diễn tả sự lịch sự/ưu tiên hiện tại.

title: Had Better

commonMistakes.right: You had better leave now.

commonMistakes.right: We had better not be late.

acceptedAnswers: He had better go home now.
choices: He had better go home now.
He had better goes home now.
He had better to go home now.
drills.explanation: After had better, the verb stays in the base form.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He had better go home now.

acceptedAnswers: You had better be careful.

drills.target: You had better be careful.

drills.target: They had better call the police.

explanation: Had better is a fixed phrase used for strong advice, warnings, or recommendations. It is followed by the base form of the verb: had better leave, had better not be late. The meaning often includes an implied bad result if the advice is ignored.
formPatterns: subject + had better not + base verb
l1Notes: Có thể nhầm had better với must hoặc should, nhưng cấu trúc quan trọng nhất là không thêm to và không chia động từ theo chủ ngữ.

title: Semi-Modals
summary: Ought to, need, and dare, and how their behaviour differs from core modals.

commonMistakes.right: You ought to apologize for being late.
commonMistakes.why: Ought to is followed by the base form of the verb, not by to plus an -ing form or a past-tense form.
commonMistakes.wrong: You ought to apologize for being late.

commonMistakes.right: You need to finish this report today.
commonMistakes.why: Need as a semi-modal takes to + base verb in affirmative statements.
commonMistakes.wrong: You need finish this report today.

commonMistakes.right: He dare not speak in the meeting.
commonMistakes.why: In formal or literary use, dare can behave like a semi-modal in negative statements without does/doing forms.
commonMistakes.wrong: He dares not speak in the meeting.

commonMistakes.right: Need you leave so early?
commonMistakes.why: As a semi-modal in questions, need can appear without do-support, especially in formal English.
commonMistakes.wrong: Do you need leave so early?

acceptedAnswers: ought to
drills.explanation: Ought to is a semi-modal phrase. It is followed by the base form of the main verb, and it shows advice or moral expectation.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: You ____ study harder if you want a higher score.
drills.target: ought to

acceptedAnswers: You ought to call your mother tonight.
drills.explanation: This sentence uses ought to for advice. The main verb after ought to is the base form call.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence giving advice. Use: ought to / call / tonight.
drills.target: You ought to call your mother tonight.

acceptedAnswers: Need you leave so early?
drills.explanation: In formal English, need can form a question without do-support. The verb after need is the base form leave.
drills.prompt: Rewrite as a question without do-support: Do you need to leave so early?
drills.target: Need you leave so early?

acceptedAnswers: You need to finish this task now.
choices: You need to finish this task now.
You need finish this task now.
You need to finishing this task now.
drills.explanation: Need as a semi-modal is followed by to + base verb in affirmative statements.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: You need to finish this task now.

acceptedAnswers: dare not
drills.explanation: Dare can behave like a semi-modal in negative statements: dare not + base verb. This is more formal or literary than the do-support form.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: He ____ tell anyone the secret.
drills.target: dare not

acceptedAnswers: He dare not tell anyone the secret.
drills.explanation: This is a semi-modal negative form. Dare is followed by the base verb tell, and the sentence does not use does not dare in this form.
drills.prompt: Write the sentence using dare as a semi-modal: he / not / tell / anyone / the secret.
drills.target: He dare not tell anyone the secret.

acceptedAnswers: He ought to be more careful.
choices: He ought to be more careful.
He ought be more careful.
He ought to being more careful.
drills.explanation: Ought to is followed by the base form be. The other options leave out to or use the wrong verb form.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He ought to be more careful.

acceptedAnswers: We need to decide today.
drills.explanation: Need in the affirmative takes to + base verb. Decide is the correct base form after to.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: We need decide today.
drills.target: We need to decide today.

acceptedAnswers: dare
drills.explanation: In the sentence pattern 'How ____ you?' with the meaning of challenge or questioning courage, dare can appear in a semi-modal style.
drills.prompt: Complete the question: How ____ you say that to her?
drills.target: dare

acceptedAnswers: Need you be so loud?
choices: Need you be so loud?
Do you need be so loud?
Need you to be so loud?
drills.explanation: With semi-modal need in a question, the base form follows need and do-support is not used. The version with to is not this semi-modal structure.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Need you be so loud?

explanation: Semi-modals are verb forms that behave partly like modal verbs but do not follow the full modal pattern. Ought to usually expresses advice or duty and is followed by the base form; need can act like a semi-modal in questions and negatives, especially in formal English; dare can also behave this way, especially in negative statements and set patterns. In normal affirmative statements, need usually takes to + base verb.
formPatterns: need + base verb in some questions/negatives
dare + base verb in some negative or fixed patterns
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt không có hệ thống bán động từ tương đương trực tiếp; người học hay quên 'to' sau need, hoặc dùng dạng chia theo ngôi như với động từ thường trong các cấu trúc semi-modal.

title: Zero Conditional
summary: General truths and cause-effect with present simple in both clauses.

commonMistakes.right: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.

commonMistakes.wrong: If you heat water to 100°C, it boil.

commonMistakes.right: If people do not sleep enough, they feel tired.

commonMistakes.wrong: If people do not sleep enough, they will feel tired.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I am late, my boss will be unhappy.

commonMistakes.right: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.

The if-clause uses the present simple, and the main clause usually uses will + base verb: If it rains, we will stay at home. The if-clause can be negative, for example If they don't leave now, they will miss the bus. In formal writing, other modal verbs can sometimes appear in the main clause, but will is the standard form at this level.
formPatterns: If + present simple, will + base verb
Will + base verb in the result clause
Don't/doesn't + base verb in the if-clause when negative

title: Second Conditional
summary: Hypothetical or unlikely present and future situations.

commonMistakes.right: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.

commonMistakes.wrong: If I have more time, I would learn Spanish.

commonMistakes.right: If she knew my address, she would write to me.
commonMistakes.why: The if-clause needs a past simple verb for this hypothetical situation. Present simple in the if-clause suggests a first conditional idea, not a second conditional one.
commonMistakes.wrong: If she knows my address, she would write to me.

commonMistakes.right: If it rained tomorrow, we would stay at home.
commonMistakes.why: Second conditional can talk about an unlikely future event. The if-clause uses past simple, not will.
commonMistakes.wrong: If it will rain tomorrow, we would stay at home.

commonMistakes.right: I would buy that car if I had enough money.
commonMistakes.why: In second conditional sentences, would goes in the main clause, not after if.
commonMistakes.wrong: I would buy that car if I would have enough money.

explanation: The second conditional describes unreal, hypothetical, or unlikely present and future situations. It usually has if + past simple, then would + base verb: If I had more time, I would travel. It is different from the first conditional, which talks about real or possible future situations and usually uses if + present simple, then will + base verb: If I have time, I will travel.

title: Third Conditional
summary: Unreal past situations and their imagined consequences.

commonMistakes.right: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
commonMistakes.why: The third conditional talks about an unreal past situation and its unreal past result. We use had + past participle in the if-clause, and would have + past participle in the result clause.
commonMistakes.wrong: If I studied harder, I would pass the exam.

commonMistakes.right: If she had left earlier, she would have caught the train.
commonMistakes.why: In the third conditional, the if-clause refers to a past situation that did not happen. We do not use would in the if-clause.
commonMistakes.wrong: If she would have left earlier, she would have caught the train.

commonMistakes.right: He would have called you if he had known your number.
commonMistakes.why: The result clause uses would have + past participle, not would + base verb, when we are talking about an unreal past result.
commonMistakes.wrong: He would call you if he had known your number.

commonMistakes.right: If we had been more careful, we would not have made that mistake.
commonMistakes.why: The third conditional needs had + past participle in the if-clause. The form would not have made shows an unreal past result.
commonMistakes.wrong: If we would be more careful, we would not make that mistake.

acceptedAnswers: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.

drills.explanation: This is the third conditional: an unreal past condition and an imagined past result. The if-clause uses had + past participle, and the result uses would have + past participle.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.

acceptedAnswers: If she had left earlier, she would have caught the train.
choices: If she had left earlier, she would catch the train.

explanation: The third conditional talks about an unreal past situation and an imagined past result. It is used when something did not happen in the past, and we imagine a different result. The usual pattern is if + past perfect in the if-clause, and would have + past participle in the main clause: If I had known, I would have helped. This contrasts with the second conditional, which talks about unreal present or future situations. Second conditional uses if + past simple and would + base verb: If I knew, I would help. So in the third conditional, both the condition and the result are in the past form, because we are imagining a different past.
explanationVi: Câu điều kiện loại 3 dùng để nói về một tình huống không có thật trong quá khứ và kết quả tưởng tượng của nó trong quá khứ. Nghĩa là: một việc đã không xảy ra, và ta tưởng tượng nếu nó đã xảy ra thì kết quả sẽ thế nào. Cấu trúc thường là If + had + V3, rồi would have + V3: If I had known, I would have helped. Đây là điểm rất dễ nhầm với câu điều kiện loại 2. Câu điều kiện loại 2 dùng cho tình huống không có thật ở hiện tại hoặc tương lai, với cấu trúc If + quá khứ đơn, would + V: If I knew, I would help. Vì vậy, loại 3 luôn mang ý nghĩa quá khứ không có thật, và cả mệnh đề if lẫn mệnh đề chính đều hướng về quá khứ. Người học tiếng Việt thường dễ bỏ had trong mệnh đề if, hoặc dùng would trong mệnh đề if, nhưng cách đó sai trong tiếng Anh chuẩn. Hãy nhớ: quá khứ không có thật thì dùng had + V3 ở vế if, và would have + V3 ở vế kết quả.
formPatterns: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.
If + had not + past participle, would not have + past participle.
Would have + past participle if + had + past participle.
Third conditional = unreal past situation + imagined past result.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường quen diễn đạt điều kiện bằng nếu... thì... mà không đổi hình thức động từ theo thời gian như tiếng Anh. Vì vậy rất dễ viết sai kiểu If I studied harder, I would have passed hoặc If I would have studied harder.... Hãy nhớ rằng loại 3 nói về quá khứ không có thật: mệnh đề if dùng had + V3, còn mệnh đề chính dùng would have + V3. So với loại 2, loại 3 không phải là giả định ở hiện tại mà là giả định ở quá khứ.

title: Mixed Conditionals
summary: Past condition with present result, or the reverse.

commonMistakes.right: If I had studied harder, I would have a better job now.
commonMistakes.why: This is a mixed conditional: the past condition (had studied harder) leads to a present result (would have a better job now).
commonMistakes.wrong: If I studied harder, I would have a better job now.

commonMistakes.right: If she had saved more money, she could travel this year.
commonMistakes.why: The condition is in the past, but the result is in the present. The wrong sentence uses a present unreal form that does not match this meaning.
commonMistakes.wrong: If she saved more money, she could travel this year.

commonMistakes.right: If we lived closer, we would have visited you last week.
commonMistakes.why: This is the reverse mixed conditional: a present condition is paired with a past result. The wrong sentence sounds like a normal unreal present conditional, not a mixed one.
commonMistakes.wrong: If we had lived closer, we would have visited you last week.

commonMistakes.right: If I were more organized, I would have finished the report on time yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: The condition is about a present habit or state, while the result is in the past. The wrong sentence uses a past condition with a past result, which is a different conditional pattern.
commonMistakes.wrong: If I had been more organized, I would have finished the report on time yesterday.

explanation:
Mixed conditionals combine a condition from one time with a result from another time. The two most common patterns are: past condition + present result (If I had studied harder, I would have a better job now) and present condition + past result (If I were more confident, I would have spoken at the meeting yesterday).

In the first pattern, the if-clause usually uses past perfect: had + past participle. The result clause usually uses would/could/might + base verb for a present result. In the second pattern, the if-clause usually uses past simple or were, and the result clause uses would/could/might have + past participle for a past result.

Be careful not to mix up mixed conditionals with normal unreal conditionals. A sentence like If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam is a normal third conditional because both parts are about the past. A sentence like If I had studied harder, I would have a better job now is mixed because the condition is past, but the result is present.
explanationVi:
Mệnh đề điều kiện hỗn hợp (mixed conditionals) dùng khi thời gian của điều kiện và thời gian của kết quả không cùng một mốc. Đây là điểm rất dễ sai vì tiếng Việt thường không bắt buộc phải đổi hình thức động từ rõ như tiếng Anh, nên người học hay dùng cùng một kiểu cho cả hai vế.

Có hai kiểu chính. Kiểu 1 là điều kiện ở quá khứ nhưng kết quả ở hiện tại: If I had studied harder, I would have a better job now. Nghĩa là việc học chăm hơn không xảy ra trong quá khứ, nhưng hậu quả vẫn còn ở hiện tại. Ở mệnh đề if, thường dùng had + V3 (quá khứ hoàn thành). Ở mệnh đề chính, thường dùng would/could/might + V nguyên mẫu để nói về kết quả hiện tại.

Kiểu 2 là điều kiện ở hiện tại nhưng kết quả ở quá khứ: If I were more confident, I would have spoken at the meeting yesterday. Nghĩa là tính chất hiện tại không có, nhưng nếu có thì quá khứ đã khác. Ở mệnh đề if, thường dùng quá khứ đơn hoặc were. Ở mệnh đề chính, dùng would/could/might have + V3 để nói về kết quả trong quá khứ.

Lỗi rất phổ biến là dùng thì giống nhau cho cả hai vế, ví dụ: If I studied harder, I would have a better job now. Câu này sai vì studied harder là kiểu điều kiện hiện tại không thật, nhưng would have a better job now lại là kết quả hiện tại; hai vế không khớp với nhau theo kiểu mixed conditional. Hãy luôn kiểm tra: điều kiện nói về quá khứ hay hiện tại, và kết quả nói về quá khứ hay hiện tại?
formPatterns: If + past perfect, would/could/might + base verb
If + past simple / were, would/could/might + have + past participle
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không đổi hình thái động từ rõ ràng để phân biệt điều kiện quá khứ và kết quả hiện tại, nên người học dễ dùng một kiểu câu cho cả hai vế. Cần chú ý rằng tiếng Anh phải đổi thì để thể hiện thời gian khác nhau giữa mệnh đề if và mệnh đề chính.

title: Unless and Provided That
summary: Alternative conditional conjunctions and their polarity traps.

commonMistakes.right: I will not go unless it stops raining.
commonMistakes.why: Unless means ‘if not’, so the clause after unless is positive. Do not use not in both clauses.
commonMistakes.wrong: I will not go unless it will not stop raining.

commonMistakes.right: You can borrow my laptop provided that you return it tomorrow.
commonMistakes.why: Provided that means ‘only if’; it introduces a condition, not a contrast or a reason.
commonMistakes.wrong: You can borrow my laptop provided that you return it yesterday.

commonMistakes.right: We will leave unless the meeting finishes early.
commonMistakes.why: After unless, use a normal present-tense condition, not will.
commonMistakes.wrong: We will leave unless the meeting will finish early.

commonMistakes.right: I will help you provided that you ask politely.
commonMistakes.why: Provided that is followed by a full, grammatical condition. It cannot be left as a fragment.
commonMistakes.wrong: I will help you provided that politely.

drills.explanation: Provided that needs a complete condition, and the clause should be grammatically parallel to the main clause.

drills.target: We will hire her provided that she has the required experience.

explanation: Unless and provided that are alternative conditional conjunctions. Unless means ‘if not’, so the clause after it is normally positive: We will go unless it rains = We will go if it does not rain. Provided that means ‘only if’ or ‘on the condition that’: You may borrow the book provided that you return it tomorrow. In both structures, avoid adding will inside the condition clause in standard English.
formPatterns: main clause + unless + positive condition clause
main clause + provided that + full condition clause
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng nếu/ trừ khi khá linh hoạt, nên người học dễ thêm phủ định hai lần hoặc dùng thì tương lai trong mệnh đề điều kiện. Nhắc rằng unless = ‘nếu không’ và provided that = ‘với điều kiện là / miễn là’.

title: Wish and If Only
summary: Regret and unreal desire, where the tense shift is counter-intuitive.

commonMistakes.right: I wish I had more time to study.
commonMistakes.why: Use past tense after wish to talk about a present situation you want to be different.
commonMistakes.wrong: I wish I have more time to study.

commonMistakes.right: She wishes she lived closer to school.
commonMistakes.why: After wish, use a past form for an unreal present situation.
commonMistakes.wrong: She wishes she lives closer to school.

commonMistakes.right: If only we knew the answer.
commonMistakes.why: If only can use a past form to express a present unreal wish.
commonMistakes.wrong: If only we know the answer.

commonMistakes.right: I wish I had not missed the bus.
commonMistakes.why: Use past perfect after wish to regret a past event.
commonMistakes.wrong: I wish I did not miss the bus.

commonMistakes.right: If only he had called me yesterday.
commonMistakes.why: Use past perfect after if only to express regret about a past event.
commonMistakes.wrong: If only he called me yesterday.

acceptedAnswers: had
drills.explanation: For an unreal present wish, we usually use wish + past simple. Here the correct verb is had.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I wish I ___ more money.
drills.target: had

acceptedAnswers: lived
drills.explanation: She wants the present situation to be different, so we use a past form after wish.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: She wishes she ___ near her office.
drills.target: lived

acceptedAnswers: were
drills.explanation: After if only, we often use were for unreal present situations, especially in formal English. Was is common in speech, but were is the standard form in lessons and tests.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: If only I ___ taller.
drills.target: were

acceptedAnswers: had left
drills.explanation: This is regret about a past event, so we use wish + past perfect.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I wish I ___ earlier.
