But many geographical names do take the: rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts, and some plural or descriptive country names such as the Netherlands, the Philippines, the United States, and the United Kingdom.

A useful exam rule is this: learn the name together with its article. Say the Nile, the Alps, the Amazon, but France, Japan, Peru. Also be careful with words like Republic, Kingdom, States, or Netherlands, because these often take the.
explanationVi:
Đây là một điểm ngữ pháp rất dễ sai vì trong tiếng Việt không có mạo từ như a/an/the. Với tên địa lý trong tiếng Anh, bạn không thể chỉ nhìn nghĩa “địa danh” mà đoán được có the hay không; nhiều trường hợp phải học theo từng loại và từng tên cụ thể.

Quy tắc cơ bản: đa số tên quốc gia không dùng the, ví dụ France, Japan, Peru. Nhưng nhiều tên địa lý khác lại dùng the, như sông, biển, đại dương, dãy núi, sa mạc. Vì vậy ta nói the Nile, the Pacific Ocean, the Alps, the Sahara. Ngoài ra, một số tên quốc gia có dạng số nhiều hoặc có cấu trúc mô tả cũng dùng the, ví dụ the Netherlands, the Philippines, the United States, the United Kingdom.

Cách nhớ tốt nhất là học cả cụm từ, không học riêng danh từ. Hãy nhớ: France nhưng the Netherlands; Japan nhưng the United States; the Nile, the Alps, the Amazon. Khi viết IELTS, lỗi thiếu the trước tên địa lý là lỗi rất phổ biến của người Việt.
formPatterns: plural or descriptive country names often with the
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt không có mạo từ nên người học hay bỏ the trước tên sông, biển, dãy núi, hoặc thêm the trước tên nước như the France, the Japan. Cần đặc biệt chú ý các tên địa lý mang tính số nhiều hoặc có từ mô tả như United, Kingdom, States, Netherlands.

title: This, That, These, Those
summary: Demonstratives for near and far reference, singular and plural.

commonMistakes.right: This book is mine.
commonMistakes.why: Use this with a singular noun that is near the speaker.
commonMistakes.wrong: These book is mine.

commonMistakes.right: Those shoes are too expensive.
commonMistakes.why: Use those with a plural noun that is far away or already mentioned.
commonMistakes.wrong: That shoes are too expensive.

commonMistakes.right: This is my phone.
commonMistakes.why: Use this for one thing near the speaker.
commonMistakes.wrong: These is my phone.

commonMistakes.right: Those are my friends.
commonMistakes.why: Use those with plural nouns. That is only for singular nouns.
commonMistakes.wrong: That are my friends.

acceptedAnswers: this
drills.explanation: This is used for one thing near the speaker.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ____ is my pen.
drills.target: this

acceptedAnswers: those
drills.explanation: Those is used for plural things far away or not near the speaker.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ____ are my shoes.
drills.target: those

acceptedAnswers: that
drills.explanation: That is used for one thing far away or already known.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ____ is your bag.
drills.target: that

acceptedAnswers: these
drills.explanation: These is used for plural things near the speaker.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ____ are my keys.
drills.target: these

acceptedAnswers: This is my sister.
choices: These is my sister.
This is my sister.
That are my sister.
drills.explanation: This matches the singular noun sister, and is is the correct verb with this.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: This is my sister.

acceptedAnswers: Those are our teachers.
choices: That are our teachers.
Those are our teachers.
These is our teachers.
drills.explanation: Those goes with the plural noun teachers, and are matches the plural subject.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Those are our teachers.

acceptedAnswers: That is my car.
choices: This are my car.
That is my car.
These is my car.
drills.explanation: That is used for one thing, and car is singular.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: That is my car.

acceptedAnswers: These are my books.
choices: This are my books.
These are my books.
Those is my books.
drills.explanation: These is used with the plural noun books, and are matches the plural subject.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: These are my books.

acceptedAnswers: This is my phone.
drills.explanation: Rewrite the sentence using the correct demonstrative for one near thing.
drills.prompt: Rewrite using this, that, these, or those: My phone is here.
drills.target: This is my phone.

acceptedAnswers: Those are my friends.
drills.explanation: Rewrite the sentence using the correct demonstrative for plural people.
drills.prompt: Rewrite using this, that, these, or those: My friends are over there.
drills.target: Those are my friends.

acceptedAnswers: This is my teacher.
drills.explanation: Build a correct sentence with this and a singular noun.
drills.prompt: Use this to make a sentence about one near person: my teacher
drills.target: This is my teacher.

acceptedAnswers: Those are new houses.
drills.explanation: Build a correct sentence with those and a plural noun.
drills.prompt: Use those to make a sentence about more than one far thing: new houses
drills.target: Those are new houses.

explanation: This, that, these, and those are demonstratives. Use this for one thing near you, that for one thing farther away or already mentioned, these for more than one thing near you, and those for more than one thing farther away or already mentioned. In English, the demonstrative normally comes before the noun, or it can stand alone before the verb be: this book, those shoes, this is my bag, those are my friends.
formPatterns: this + singular noun / this + be + singular noun
that + singular noun / that + be + singular noun
these + plural noun / these + be + plural noun
those + plural noun / those + be + plural noun
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không bắt buộc phân biệt rõ gần/xa và số ít/số nhiều bằng từ chỉ định như tiếng Anh, nên người học dễ dùng nhầm this/that/these/those hoặc quên đổi động từ be theo số ít/số nhiều.

title: Some and Any
summary: Non-specific quantity across affirmative, negative, and interrogative forms.

commonMistakes.right: I have some water in my bag.
commonMistakes.why: Use some in affirmative sentences when the amount is indefinite or not important. Any is not used in this kind of positive statement.
commonMistakes.wrong: I have any water in my bag.

commonMistakes.right: I do not have any money.
commonMistakes.why: Use any in negative sentences. Some is usually not correct in a standard negative statement.
commonMistakes.wrong: I do not have some money.

commonMistakes.right: Do you have any questions?
commonMistakes.why: Use any in most questions about an indefinite amount or number. Some is less common in general questions.
commonMistakes.wrong: Do you have some questions?

commonMistakes.right: Would you like some tea?
commonMistakes.why: Use some in offers and requests, because the speaker expects or wants a positive answer.
commonMistakes.wrong: Would you like any tea?

acceptedAnswers: some
drills.explanation: Use some in positive sentences for an indefinite amount.
drills.prompt: I have ____ rice at home.
drills.target: some

acceptedAnswers: any
drills.explanation: Use any in negative sentences.
drills.prompt: We do not have ____ eggs.
drills.target: any

acceptedAnswers: any
drills.explanation: Use any in questions about an indefinite amount.
drills.prompt: Do you have ____ brothers?
drills.target: any

acceptedAnswers: some
drills.explanation: Use some in offers and requests.
drills.prompt: Would you like ____ water?
drills.target: some

acceptedAnswers: I have some friends in London.
drills.explanation: This is a positive sentence, so some is correct.
drills.prompt: Write a correct sentence: I / have / some / friends / in London
drills.target: I have some friends in London.

acceptedAnswers: I do not have any time today.
drills.explanation: In a negative sentence, any is the correct choice.
drills.prompt: Write a correct sentence: I / do not have / any / time / today
drills.target: I do not have any time today.

acceptedAnswers: Do you have any homework?
drills.explanation: Questions about an indefinite amount usually take any.
drills.prompt: Write a correct question: you / have / any / homework
drills.target: Do you have any homework?

acceptedAnswers: Would you like some soup?
drills.explanation: Offers commonly use some, not any.
drills.prompt: Write a correct question: Would you like / some / soup
drills.target: Would you like some soup?

acceptedAnswers: There are some books on the table.
drills.explanation: In an affirmative sentence, some is correct before a plural noun.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with the correct determiner: There are books on the table.
drills.target: There are some books on the table.

acceptedAnswers: There are not any books on the table.
drills.explanation: In a negative sentence, any is correct before a plural noun.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with the correct determiner: There are not books on the table.
drills.target: There are not any books on the table.

acceptedAnswers: Choose some milk.
choices: Choose any milk.
Choose some milk.
Choose many milk.
drills.explanation: Some is correct for an offer or request. Any is wrong here.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Choose some milk.

acceptedAnswers: Are there any apples?
choices: Are there some apples?
Are there any apples?
Is there any apples?
drills.explanation: Any is the natural choice in this question about number.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Are there any apples?

acceptedAnswers: I need some help.
choices: I need any help.
I need some help.
I need a help.
drills.explanation: Some is used in an affirmative statement with an uncountable noun.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I need some help.

acceptedAnswers: He does not want any sugar.
choices: He does not want some sugar.
He does not want any sugar.
He does not want a sugar.
drills.explanation: Any is correct in the negative sentence.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He does not want any sugar.

explanation: Some and any are used with indefinite amounts or numbers. Use some in affirmative sentences, and also in offers and requests. Use any in negative sentences and usually in questions. With uncountable nouns like water, rice, sugar, and help, and with plural nouns like books or apples, the same rule still applies.
explanationVi: Some và any đều dùng để nói về số lượng không xác định, khi người nói không nêu rõ là bao nhiêu. Quy tắc cơ bản là: dùng some trong câu khẳng định, và cũng dùng some trong lời mời, lời đề nghị, hoặc yêu cầu lịch sự. Dùng any trong câu phủ định và thường dùng any trong câu hỏi. Quy tắc này áp dụng cho cả danh từ không đếm được như water, rice, sugar, help và danh từ số nhiều như books, apples. Người Việt học tiếng Anh hay bị ảnh hưởng bởi cách dùng “một ít / vài” trong tiếng Việt nên thường dùng some hoặc any theo nghĩa, nhưng trong tiếng Anh phải nhìn vào loại câu trước tiên: khẳng định thì thường là some, phủ định thì any, câu hỏi thì thường any, còn lời mời/lời đề nghị thì some.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt không có hệ thống some/any tương đương trực tiếp, nên người học hay dịch từng từ như “một vài”, “một ít” và bỏ qua loại câu. Lỗi phổ biến là dùng any trong câu khẳng định hoặc dùng some trong câu hỏi phủ định; cần nhớ rằng trong tiếng Anh, từ quyết định chủ yếu là cấu trúc câu, không chỉ là nghĩa của số lượng.

title: No and None
summary: Zero quantity as a determiner and as a pronoun.

commonMistakes.right: I have no time today.
commonMistakes.why: Use no before a noun to mean zero quantity. Do not use not with a noun here.
commonMistakes.wrong: I have not time today.

commonMistakes.right: There are no tickets left.
commonMistakes.why: No comes before the plural noun tickets to show that there are zero tickets.
commonMistakes.wrong: There are not tickets left.

commonMistakes.right: I have no money with me.
commonMistakes.why: No is a determiner before money. None cannot directly modify a noun.
commonMistakes.wrong: I have none money with me.

commonMistakes.right: I asked for help, but none was available.
commonMistakes.why: None is a pronoun and can stand alone. Use no + noun when a noun follows, and none when the noun is omitted.
commonMistakes.wrong: I asked for help, but no was available.

acceptedAnswers: no
drills.explanation: Use no before a noun to show zero quantity.
drills.prompt: We have ____ chairs in the room.
drills.target: no

acceptedAnswers: none
drills.explanation: None is used as a pronoun when it stands alone.
drills.prompt: How many apples are left? ____
drills.target: none

acceptedAnswers: There are no eggs in the fridge.
choices: There are no eggs in the fridge.
There are not eggs in the fridge.
There are none eggs in the fridge.
drills.explanation: No goes directly before the noun eggs to show zero quantity.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: There are no eggs in the fridge.

acceptedAnswers: I have no idea.
drills.explanation: No can be used before a noun phrase such as idea.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with no to say that you do not know the answer: idea / I / have / no
drills.target: I have no idea.

acceptedAnswers: None of the students was late.
drills.explanation: None can mean not any of a group. With of the students, none works as the pronoun before the verb.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using none: Not any of the students was late.
drills.target: None of the students was late.

acceptedAnswers: No one came to the meeting.
choices: No one came to the meeting.
None came to the meeting.
Not one came to the meeting.
drills.explanation: No one is the correct pronoun for people here. None is not used before a verb without of.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: No one came to the meeting.

acceptedAnswers: none
drills.explanation: None can replace a noun phrase when the meaning is zero.
drills.prompt: We asked for volunteers, but ____ were available.
drills.target: none

acceptedAnswers: There is no problem.
drills.explanation: No can be used before a singular noun to show that nothing is wrong or present.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with no meaning zero quantity: problem / there / is / no
drills.target: There is no problem.

acceptedAnswers: I have no siblings.
choices: I have no siblings.
I have none siblings.
I have not siblings.
drills.explanation: No comes directly before the noun siblings. None cannot modify siblings.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I have no siblings.

explanation: No is a determiner, and it comes directly before a noun: no time, no money, no tickets. None is a pronoun, so it stands alone or appears in phrases like none of them. In negative meaning, English usually uses no + noun or none, not not + noun.
l1Notes: Người Việt hay dùng phủ định trực tiếp với danh từ theo kiểu không có + danh từ, nên dễ viết sai thành not time / not tickets. Hãy nhớ: tiếng Anh thường dùng no trước danh từ hoặc none thay cho cả cụm danh từ.

title: Each and Every
summary: Individual versus collective totality, both taking a singular verb.

commonMistakes.right: Each student has a laptop.
commonMistakes.why: Each means every person or thing separately, so the verb is singular. In Vietnamese, learners often use a plural idea with a plural verb.
commonMistakes.wrong: Each student have a laptop.

commonMistakes.right: Every day is busy for me.
commonMistakes.why: Every is followed by a singular noun and takes a singular verb. Do not use a plural verb after every.
commonMistakes.wrong: Every day are busy for me.

commonMistakes.right: Each of the books is interesting.
commonMistakes.why: After each of, the verb is singular because the subject is still treated one by one. The noun after of is plural, but the verb is not.
commonMistakes.wrong: Each of the books are interesting.

commonMistakes.right: Every student in the class needs a book.
commonMistakes.why: Every is used with a singular noun, even when it refers to all members of a group. The verb must also be singular.
commonMistakes.wrong: Every students in the class need a book.

acceptedAnswers: Each
drills.explanation: Use each when you mean the members of a group separately, one by one.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ____ student must bring an ID card.
drills.target: Each

acceptedAnswers: Every
drills.explanation: Use every before a singular noun to mean all members of a group.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ____ morning, I drink coffee.
drills.target: Every

acceptedAnswers: Each child needs a ticket.
drills.explanation: Each makes the subject singular, so the verb is needs, not need.
drills.prompt: Write a correct sentence using: each / child / need / a ticket
drills.target: Each child needs a ticket.

acceptedAnswers: Every room was clean.
drills.explanation: Every is followed by a singular noun, and the verb is singular past tense.
drills.prompt: Write a correct sentence using: every / room / be / clean
drills.target: Every room was clean.

acceptedAnswers: Each of the teams is ready.
drills.explanation: Each of the + plural noun still takes a singular verb because each focuses on individual members.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with each of the: The teams are ready.
drills.target: Each of the teams is ready.

acceptedAnswers: Every student in the class has a phone.
choices: Every student in the class have a phone.
Every students in the class has a phone.
Every student in the class has a phone.
drills.explanation: Every is followed by a singular noun, so has is correct and the other forms are not.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Every student in the class has a phone.

acceptedAnswers: Each of the apples is ripe.
choices: Each of the apples are ripe.
Each of the apples is ripe.
Each of the apple is ripe.
drills.explanation: Each of the plus a plural noun takes a singular verb, and apples must stay plural.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Each of the apples is ripe.

acceptedAnswers: Each person pays for their own ticket.
drills.explanation: Each can be used with a singular idea about separate people, so pays is singular. Their own ticket is acceptable in modern English for an individual meaning.
drills.prompt: Write a correct sentence about separate people paying individually.
drills.target: Each person pays for their own ticket.

acceptedAnswers: Every car in the showroom was expensive.
drills.explanation: Every takes a singular noun and a singular verb, even when the meaning is a whole group.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: Every car in the showroom were expensive.
drills.target: Every car in the showroom was expensive.

explanation: Each and every both refer to all members of a group, but they focus on them in different ways. Each stresses individual items or people one by one; every stresses the whole group. Both are followed by a singular noun and usually take a singular verb: each student is, every student is. In structures like each of the books and every one of the books, the verb is still singular because the subject is treated as singular. Every can also be used for repeated time expressions such as every day, every week, and every year.
formPatterns: each of + plural noun + singular verb
every one of + plural noun + singular verb
every + time expression: every day, every week, every year
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không bắt buộc hòa hợp số với động từ như tiếng Anh, nên người học dễ viết verb số nhiều sau each/every. Cũng dễ nhầm vì cả hai đều có thể dịch là mỗi / mọi / từng, nhưng trong tiếng Anh chúng vẫn đi với danh từ số ít và động từ số ít.

title: Regular Plurals
summary: Plural -s and its spelling variants. Vietnamese does not inflect nouns for number.

commonMistakes.right: I have two books on my desk.
commonMistakes.why: Plural count nouns usually need -s or -es when the number is more than one.
commonMistakes.wrong: I have two book on my desk.

commonMistakes.right: The bus is late this morning.
commonMistakes.why: Some singular nouns end in -s, so not every final -s means a plural.
commonMistakes.wrong: The buss is late this morning.

commonMistakes.right: She bought three boxes of apples.
commonMistakes.why: After nouns ending in -s, -x, -ch, -sh, or -z, we usually add -es to make the plural.
commonMistakes.wrong: She bought three boxs of apples.

commonMistakes.right: There are many people in the room.
commonMistakes.why: Some common plurals are irregular and do not take regular -s.
commonMistakes.wrong: There are many peoples in the room.

acceptedAnswers: cats
drills.explanation: Most regular plural nouns add -s to the singular form.
drills.prompt: Write the plural form of cat: cat → ____
drills.target: cats

acceptedAnswers: boxes
drills.explanation: Nouns ending in -x usually add -es to make the plural.
drills.prompt: Write the plural form of box: box → ____
drills.target: boxes

acceptedAnswers: buses
drills.explanation: Nouns ending in -s often take -es in the plural.
drills.prompt: Write the plural form of bus: bus → ____
drills.target: buses

acceptedAnswers: babies
drills.explanation: After a consonant + y, we change y to i and add -es.
drills.prompt: Write the plural form of baby: baby → ____
drills.target: babies

acceptedAnswers: dogs are in the garden.
drills.explanation: The noun dog is plural here, so it needs -s.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with a plural noun: The dog is in the garden.
drills.target: dogs are in the garden.

acceptedAnswers: I have three oranges.
drills.explanation: With a number greater than one, the count noun takes the plural form.
drills.prompt: Use these words to make a correct sentence: I / have / three / orange
drills.target: I have three oranges.

acceptedAnswers: She has two pencils.
Choose the correct sentence.
choices: She has two pencil.
She has two pencils.
She has two pencilses.
drills.explanation: After a number, a regular count noun must be plural.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She has two pencils.

acceptedAnswers: There are many children in the park.
Choose the correct sentence.
choices: There are many childs in the park.
There are many children in the park.
There are many child in the park.
drills.explanation: Child is irregular, so its plural is children, not childs or child.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: There are many children in the park.

acceptedAnswers: The boxes are on the table.
drills.explanation: The plural of box is boxes, with -es added after -x.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: The box are on the table.
drills.target: The boxes are on the table.

acceptedAnswers: The babies are sleeping.
drills.explanation: After consonant + y, the plural changes y to i and adds -es.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: The babys are sleeping.
drills.target: The babies are sleeping.

acceptedAnswers: I bought two dresses.
choices: I bought two dress.
I bought two dresses.
I bought two dresss.
drills.explanation: Dresses is the correct plural form of dress.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I bought two dresses.

acceptedAnswers: She has four classes today.
drills.explanation: Class is a regular noun that takes -es in the plural because it ends in -s.
drills.prompt: Use these words to make a correct sentence: She / have / four / class / today
drills.target: She has four classes today.

acceptedAnswers: The buses are late.
drills.explanation: Bus forms the plural with -es, not just -s.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with a plural noun: The bus is late.
drills.target: The buses are late.

acceptedAnswers: I saw three dogs and two cats.
drills.explanation: Both dog and cat need regular plural -s after the numbers three and two.
drills.prompt: Use these words to make a correct sentence: I / see / three / dog / and / two / cat
drills.target: I saw three dogs and two cats.

explanation: Regular plurals are usually formed with -s: book → books, dog → dogs. After some endings, the spelling changes: box → boxes, bus → buses, baby → babies. In English, count nouns usually need a plural form after numbers greater than one. This is different from Vietnamese, where nouns do not usually change form for singular and plural, so learners often forget the -s or use the singular after a number.
explanationVi: Trong tiếng Anh, danh từ đếm được thường phải đổi sang số nhiều khi nói về hơn một người/vật. Cách phổ biến nhất là thêm -s: book → books, dog → dogs. Nhưng có các quy tắc chính tả khác: danh từ tận cùng bằng -x, -s, -sh, -ch thường thêm -es, ví dụ box → boxes, bus → buses; danh từ tận cùng bằng phụ âm + y thì đổi y thành i rồi thêm -es, ví dụ baby → babies. Sau số lượng như two, three, many, several, danh từ đếm được thường phải ở dạng số nhiều: two books, three boxes. Lỗi rất phổ biến của người Việt là dùng nguyên dạng số ít vì tiếng Việt không biến đổi danh từ theo số ít/số nhiều. Cần nhớ rằng không phải mọi từ có -s cuối đều là số nhiều: có những danh từ số ít như bus trong dạng gốc và một số danh từ số nhiều bất quy tắc như children. Tuy vậy, trong bài này trọng tâm là quy tắc số nhiều thông thường.

l1Notes: Tiếng Việt không bắt buộc đổi hình thức danh từ để biểu thị số ít/số nhiều, nên người học rất dễ quên thêm -s/-es hoặc vẫn dùng dạng số ít sau số lượng.

explanationVi: Trong tiếng Anh, nhiều danh từ số nhiều không thêm -s hoặc -es như bình thường. Đây là các dạng bất quy tắc cần học thuộc vì không thể đoán chỉ bằng quy tắc chung. Ví dụ: child → children, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice, man → men, person → people, criterion → criteria. Người học tiếng Việt thường bị ảnh hưởng bởi thói quen “đã nhiều thì thêm -s”, nên dễ nói sai như childs, foots, tooths. Hãy nhớ rằng trong tiếng Anh, một số danh từ đổi hẳn hình thức ở số nhiều, và động từ đi kèm cũng phải đổi theo số nhiều: children are, feet are, people are. title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
summary: The countability distinction that drives articles, quantifiers, and agreement.

commonMistakes.right: I need some information about the course.

commonMistakes.wrong: I need an information about the course.

commonMistakes.right: There are many students in the library.

commonMistakes.wrong: There is many student in the library.

commonMistakes.wrong: I bought a bread and a cheese.

explanation: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms and can be counted: one apple, two apples, many apples. Uncountable nouns do not normally have a plural form and do not take ‘a/an’ directly: water, advice, homework, furniture, information, rice, sugar. With countable nouns, use many, few, a few, and numbers. With uncountable nouns, use much, little, a little, some, a lot of, or a measure phrase such as a piece of advice, a bottle of water, or a loaf of bread. Verb agreement also follows countability: There is some milk. There are five chairs. In Vietnamese, many learners try to count uncountable nouns directly, so they write forms like an information, many homework, or a rice. In English, the noun itself decides which article, quantifier, and verb form is correct.
explanationVi: Danh từ đếm được có hình thức số ít và số nhiều, và có thể đếm được: one apple, two apples, many apples. Danh từ không đếm được thường không có số nhiều và không dùng trực tiếp với a/an: water, advice, homework, furniture, information, rice, sugar. Với danh từ đếm được, dùng many, few, a few và số đếm. Với danh từ không đếm được, dùng much, little, a little, some, a lot of, hoặc cụm đo lường như a piece of advice, a bottle of water, a loaf of bread. Sự hòa hợp với động từ cũng phụ thuộc vào tính đếm được: There is some milk. There are five chairs. Người học tiếng Việt thường chuyển thẳng cách nói kiểu ‘một thông tin’, ‘nhiều bài tập về nhà’, hoặc ‘một cơm/rice’ sang tiếng Anh, nhưng trong tiếng Anh chính tính đếm được của danh từ quyết định mạo từ, lượng từ và dạng động từ.
formPatterns: Measure phrase: a piece of / a bottle of / a loaf of + uncountable noun
Agreement: There is + uncountable singular idea; There are + countable plural noun
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không bắt buộc phân biệt đếm được/không đếm được bằng hình thái danh từ, nên người học dễ nói ‘một thông tin’, ‘nhiều homework’, ‘một rice’. Cần nhớ: trong tiếng Anh, không đếm được thì không dùng a/an trực tiếp và thường đi với much/some/a little hoặc cụm đơn vị đo lường.

explanation: Much and many both talk about quantity, but they are used with different noun types. Use many with countable nouns in plural form: many books, many students, many questions. Use much with uncountable nouns: much water, much money, much time, much rice. In everyday affirmative sentences, English often prefers a lot of or lots of instead of much, but much is common in questions and negatives. A useful IELTS rule is: if you can count the items one by one, use many; if you cannot count them separately, use much.
explanationVi: Much và many đều dùng để nói về số lượng, nhưng chúng đi với hai loại danh từ khác nhau. Many dùng với danh từ đếm được số nhiều: many books, many students, many questions. Much dùng với danh từ không đếm được: much water, much money, much time, much rice. Trong câu khẳng định hằng ngày, tiếng Anh thường thích a lot of hoặc lots of hơn much, nhưng much rất thường gặp trong câu hỏi và câu phủ định. Mẹo nhớ cho IELTS: nếu bạn có thể đếm từng cái một, dùng many; nếu không thể đếm riêng từng phần, dùng much.

explanation:
A few and a little both mean a small quantity, but they are used with different noun types. Use a few with plural countable nouns: a few books, a few friends, a few questions. Use a little with uncountable nouns: a little water, a little time, a little money.

The article changes the meaning. A few and a little are usually positive: they mean some, and often enough for the situation. Few and little without a are usually negative: they mean not many or not much. Compare: I have a few friends = some friends; I have few friends = not many friends. I have a little time = some time; I have little time = not much time.

This is different from much and many. Many is for plural countable nouns, and much is for uncountable nouns. In positive statements, English often prefers a few and a little instead of many and much. For example, I have a few friends is more natural than I have many friends in everyday speech. I have a little money is more natural than I have much money in everyday speech. Much and many are common in questions and negatives: Do you have many friends? I don’t have much time.
explanationVi:
A few và a little đều có nghĩa là “một ít / một vài”, nhưng dùng với loại danh từ khác nhau. A few đi với danh từ đếm được số nhiều: a few books, a few friends, a few questions. A little đi với danh từ không đếm được: a little water, a little time, a little money.

Điểm rất quan trọng là có mạo từ a hay không. A few và a little thường mang nghĩa tích cực: “có một ít”, và thường là đủ cho tình huống đó. Few và little không có a thường mang nghĩa tiêu cực: “không nhiều”, “không đủ”. So sánh: I have a few friends = tôi có vài người bạn; I have few friends = tôi có rất ít bạn, nghe hơi buồn và nhấn mạnh là không nhiều. I have a little time = tôi có một chút thời gian; I have little time = tôi có rất ít thời gian.

Phân biệt với much và many: many đi với danh từ đếm được số nhiều, much đi với danh từ không đếm được. Nhưng trong câu khẳng định, tiếng Anh thường thích dùng a few và a little hơn much/many. Ví dụ: I have a few friends tự nhiên hơn I have many friends trong giao tiếp hằng ngày. I have a little money tự nhiên hơn I have much money. Much và many rất hay dùng trong câu hỏi và câu phủ định: Do you have many friends? I don’t have much time.
formPatterns: few + plural countable noun = not many
l1Notes: Người Việt thường dịch thẳng “một ít” cho cả danh từ đếm được và không đếm được, nên dễ nhầm a few với a little. Cũng dễ quên rằng bỏ a đi thì few/little đổi sang nghĩa tiêu cực: few = rất ít, little = rất ít (gần như không đủ).

title: Compound Nouns
summary: Two nouns forming one idea, and which part takes the plural.

commonMistakes.wrong: I bought two teethbrushes yesterday.

commonMistakes.wrong: She works in a coffees shop near my house.

commonMistakes.why: When a compound noun is used as an adjective before another noun, it is usually hyphenated.
commonMistakes.wrong: We rented a three bedroom apartment.

commonMistakes.wrong: My sister bought a pair of sunglass.

drills.explanation: Toothbrush is a compound noun. The first part stays singular, and the plural ending goes on the last word.

drills.target: This is a two-hour exam.

acceptedAnswers: sunglasses

choices: I need new headphone for my laptop.

explanation: Compound nouns combine two nouns to make one idea, such as toothbrush, coffee shop, and bus stop. In most noun+noun compounds, the first noun stays singular and the plural ending goes on the last noun: toothbrushes, coffee shops, bus stops. Some compounds are written as one word, some as two words, and some with a hyphen. When the compound comes before another noun as an adjective, it is often hyphenated: a two-bedroom apartment, a three-hour meeting. Some compound nouns are always plural in form, such as sunglasses and headphones.
formPatterns: Noun + noun compounds usually take the plural on the final noun: bus stops, coffee shops, toothbrushes.
Some compound nouns are one word, some are two words, and some are hyphenated.
Compound adjectives before a noun are often hyphenated: a two-hour exam, a three-bedroom flat.
Some nouns are plural in form even for one item: sunglasses, headphones.

title: Collective Nouns

title: Quantifier Of-Phrases
summary: A piece of, a slice of, and other partitives for uncountables.

commonMistakes.right: I bought a piece of advice from my mentor.
commonMistakes.why: Advice is uncountable, so we use a partitive phrase like a piece of advice. A sentence like this without the partitive is wrong because advice cannot normally be counted directly.
commonMistakes.wrong: I bought an advice from my mentor.

commonMistakes.right: She gave me a slice of cake after dinner.
commonMistakes.why: Cake is usually an uncountable mass noun, so slice of is a natural partitive. The phrase a slice of cake is correct; cake alone would not fit in the same sentence if the meaning is one portion.
commonMistakes.wrong: She gave me a slice cake after dinner.

commonMistakes.right: We need a bit of patience in this job.
commonMistakes.why: Patience is uncountable, so it needs a partitive such as a bit of. Using a directly before patience is not grammatical.
commonMistakes.wrong: We need a patience in this job.

commonMistakes.right: He asked for a piece of information at the office.
commonMistakes.why: Information is uncountable in standard English, so piece of information is the correct partitive. It cannot normally take a direct singular count form here.
commonMistakes.wrong: He asked for an information at the office.

commonMistakes.wrong: They made a three-years contract.

title: Adverb Position
summary: Front, mid, and end position, and how position changes emphasis.

explanation: Adverb position depends on the type of adverb and the verb in the sentence. In B1 English, frequency adverbs like usually, often, always, and never normally go before the main verb, but after be. Adverbs of certainty like probably usually go before the main verb and after be. Some adverbs can also move to the front of the sentence for emphasis, especially in storytelling or formal writing. End position is also common, especially with manner or time adverbs, and the position can change what sounds natural or what is emphasized.

explanation:
Many adjectives with -ed and -ing come in pairs. The -ing form usually describes the thing, person, event, or situation that causes a feeling; the -ed form usually describes the person who feels the emotion. So a movie can be boring, and you can be bored. A lesson can be confusing, and you can be confused. A news story can be surprising, and you can be surprised.

A useful test is to ask: “What causes the feeling?” If the noun causes the feeling, use -ing. If the noun is the person who feels it, use -ed. This pattern is very common in IELTS writing and speaking, especially with boring/bored, interesting/interested, tiring/tired, exciting/excited, confusing/confused, and surprising/surprised.

Be careful: not every -ed adjective is about feelings, and some adjectives with -ed can have other meanings, especially in fixed expressions. But for this grammar point, the main contrast is cause versus feeling.
explanationVi:
Trong tiếng Anh, rất nhiều tính từ có hai dạng gần giống nhau: -ing và -ed. Cách dùng thường là: -ing để nói về thứ “gây ra cảm giác”, còn -ed để nói về người “cảm thấy” cảm giác đó. Ví dụ: the movie was boring = bộ phim làm bạn chán; I was bored = tôi cảm thấy chán. Tương tự: interesting/interested, tiring/tired, exciting/excited, confusing/confused, surprising/surprised.

Một cách kiểm tra rất hiệu quả là hỏi: “Cái gì gây ra cảm giác này?” Nếu danh từ đó là nguyên nhân, dùng -ing. Nếu danh từ đó là người đang cảm thấy, dùng -ed. Đây là lỗi rất hay gặp của người Việt vì trong tiếng Việt ta thường chỉ nói “chán”, “thú vị”, “mệt”, “hào hứng”, không có sự thay đổi hình thức tính từ để phân biệt nguyên nhân và cảm xúc như tiếng Anh. Ví dụ: “bộ phim chán” có thể khiến người học viết sai thành the movie was bored, nhưng đúng phải là the movie was boring. Ngược lại, “tôi chán” phải là I was bored, không phải I was boring.

Trong IELTS, lỗi này rất dễ làm mất điểm ngữ pháp cơ bản. Hãy nhớ: người = -ed, vật/sự việc gây cảm xúc = -ing. Tuy nhiên, một số tính từ -ed không chỉ nói về cảm xúc mà còn có nghĩa khác trong vài ngữ cảnh cố định, nên cần xem theo ngữ cảnh cụ thể. Nhưng với điểm ngữ pháp này, quy tắc chính vẫn là: nguyên nhân dùng -ing, cảm xúc dùng -ed.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không đổi hình thức tính từ để phân biệt “nguyên nhân gây cảm xúc” và “người/đối tượng đang có cảm xúc”, nên người học dễ viết sai kiểu “bộ phim bị chán” hoặc “tôi rất boring”. Cần nhớ: tiếng Anh dùng -ing cho nguyên nhân và -ed cho cảm xúc.

title: Gradable and Non-Gradable
summary: Why very freezing fails and absolutely freezing works.

commonMistakes.right: The weather is very cold today.
commonMistakes.why: Cold is a gradable adjective, so we can use very with it.
commonMistakes.wrong: The weather is very freezing today.

commonMistakes.right: The film was absolutely amazing.
commonMistakes.why: Amazing is a strong adjective, so absolutely is natural with it. Very is also possible in some contexts, but absolutely is more typical.
commonMistakes.wrong: The film was very amazing.

commonMistakes.right: I am a little tired after work.
commonMistakes.why: Tired is gradable, so it can take a degree like a little, quite, or very.
commonMistakes.wrong: I am a little exhausted after work.

commonMistakes.right: The room was completely empty.
commonMistakes.why: Empty is often treated as a non-gradable adjective in this meaning, so completely fits better than very.
commonMistakes.wrong: The room was very empty.

acceptedAnswers: very cold
drills.explanation: Cold is gradable, so it can be modified by very.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: The water is ____ cold.
drills.target: very cold

acceptedAnswers: absolutely freezing
drills.explanation: Freezing is used as a strong, non-gradable adjective here, so absolutely is the natural modifier.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: It is ____ freezing outside.
drills.target: absolutely freezing

acceptedAnswers: extremely tired
drills.explanation: Tired is gradable, so an intensifier like extremely can modify it.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: She looked ____ tired after the exam.
drills.target: extremely tired

acceptedAnswers: completely impossible
drills.explanation: Impossible is non-gradable in this sense, so completely is appropriate.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: The task was ____ impossible.
drills.target: completely impossible

acceptedAnswers: The soup is very hot.
choices: The soup is very hot.
The soup is very boiling.
The soup is absolutely hot.
drills.explanation: Hot is gradable, so very hot is correct. Boiling and absolutely hot are not natural here.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The soup is very hot.

acceptedAnswers: The test was absolutely terrible.
choices: The test was very terrible.
The test was absolutely terrible.
The test was quite terrible.
drills.explanation: Terrible is a strong adjective, so absolutely terrible is natural. Very terrible is generally not idiomatic.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The test was absolutely terrible.

acceptedAnswers: I was a bit nervous before the interview.
choices: I was a bit nervous before the interview.
I was a bit terrified before the interview.
I was absolutely nervous before the interview.
drills.explanation: Nervous is gradable, so a bit is possible. Absolutely nervous is not natural in standard English.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I was a bit nervous before the interview.

acceptedAnswers: The door is completely open.
choices: The door is very open.
The door is completely open.
The door is extremely open.
drills.explanation: Open can be used as a non-gradable result state in this context, so completely open is natural. Very open is often unnatural here.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The door is completely open.

acceptedAnswers: The answer is almost impossible.
drills.explanation: Almost can modify non-gradable adjectives to mean 'nearly', which is natural here.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using almost: The answer is impossible.
drills.target: The answer is almost impossible.

acceptedAnswers: The movie was really good.
drills.explanation: Good is gradable, so really can modify it naturally.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using really: The movie was good.
drills.target: The movie was really good.

acceptedAnswers: absolutely
drills.explanation: Absolutely commonly goes with strong or non-gradable adjectives such as impossible, amazing, or freezing.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The result was ____ impossible.
drills.target: absolutely

acceptedAnswers: very
drills.explanation: Very is used with gradable adjectives like cold, tired, and hot.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The weather is ____ cold today.
drills.target: very

explanation: Gradable adjectives describe qualities that can vary in degree, so they naturally take modifiers like very, quite, rather, a bit, or extremely: very cold, quite tired, extremely good. Non-gradable adjectives express a strong or absolute meaning, so they usually do not combine with very. They often go with absolutely, completely, totally, or nearly: absolutely freezing, completely impossible, totally exhausted. Some adjectives can be used in more than one way depending on meaning and context, so the rule is about typical use, not an absolute ban in every sentence.
formPatterns: a bit / quite / rather + gradable adjective
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng rất với cả tính từ mức độ và tính từ mang nghĩa mạnh, nên người học dễ nói very freezing hoặc very impossible. Trong tiếng Anh, những tính từ đã mang nghĩa cực độ như freezing, impossible, exhausted thường đi với absolutely, completely, totally hơn là very.

title: Intensifiers
summary: Quite, rather, fairly, and pretty, with their strength ordering.

commonMistakes.right: The hotel was quite expensive.
commonMistakes.why: Quite can mean a moderate degree here, but it is not as strong as very. The sentence is correct; this mistake is usually about choosing the wrong intensifier for the intended strength.
commonMistakes.wrong: The hotel was very expensive.

commonMistakes.right: The test was rather difficult.
commonMistakes.why: Rather often means quite or fairly and can sound a little stronger than fairly. It is not the same as very.
commonMistakes.wrong: The test was very difficult.

commonMistakes.right: The room is fairly clean.
commonMistakes.why: Fairly means moderately or to a moderate degree. It is weaker than very.
commonMistakes.wrong: The room is very clean.

commonMistakes.right: The film was pretty good.
commonMistakes.why: Pretty is an informal intensifier meaning fairly or quite. It does not mean 'beautiful' in this sentence.
commonMistakes.wrong: The film was pretty beautiful.

acceptedAnswers: fairly
drills.explanation: Fairly is used before adjectives and adverbs to mean 'to a moderate degree.'
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The restaurant was _____ busy.
drills.target: fairly

acceptedAnswers: rather
drills.explanation: Rather is an intensifier meaning 'quite' or 'fairly,' often with a slightly stronger or more surprising feeling than fairly.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The exam was _____ hard.
drills.target: rather

acceptedAnswers: pretty
drills.explanation: Pretty can mean 'fairly' or 'quite' in informal English.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: She is _____ confident about the interview.
drills.target: pretty

acceptedAnswers: quite
drills.explanation: Quite is a common intensifier meaning 'to a fairly large degree' in British English and often 'completely' with some adjectives, but here it means 'fairly.'
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The service was _____ good.
drills.target: quite

acceptedAnswers: The room was fairly quiet.
choices: The room was quite quiet.
The room was fairly quiet.
The room was very quiet.
drills.explanation: Fairly is the best fit for a moderate degree. The other options are stronger intensifiers.
drills.prompt: Choose the sentence that best matches a moderate degree of quietness.
drills.target: The room was fairly quiet.

acceptedAnswers: The movie was rather long.
choices: The movie was fairly long.
The movie was rather long.
The movie was very long.
drills.explanation: Rather is a correct intensifier here and is a little stronger than fairly.
drills.prompt: Choose the sentence that uses rather correctly.
drills.target: The movie was rather long.

acceptedAnswers: The soup was pretty hot.
choices: The soup was pretty hot.
The soup was pretty hottest.
The soup was prettily hot.
drills.explanation: Pretty can modify an adjective like hot. The other options are not grammatical in this meaning.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The soup was pretty hot.

acceptedAnswers: The tickets are quite cheap.
choices: The tickets are fairly cheap.
The tickets are quite cheap.
The tickets are very cheap.
drills.explanation: All three can be grammatical, but quite fits the target meaning best here and is included as the correct choice. It shows a moderate or fairly strong degree, depending on context and variety of English.
drills.prompt: Choose the sentence that best fits the idea of 'to some degree, but not extremely.'
drills.target: The tickets are quite cheap.

acceptedAnswers: The weather is fairly warm.
drills.explanation: This transforms the idea into a sentence using fairly correctly before an adjective.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using fairly: The weather is moderately warm.
drills.target: The weather is fairly warm.

acceptedAnswers: The flight was rather expensive.
drills.explanation: Rather is a natural intensifier before an adjective in a full sentence.
drills.prompt: Use the words to make a correct sentence: flight / rather / expensive / was / the
drills.target: The flight was rather expensive.

explanation: Intensifiers like quite, rather, fairly, and pretty are used before adjectives and adverbs to show degree. For this lesson, think of fairly as the weakest, pretty and quite as medium, and rather as a little stronger or more marked than fairly. Exact strength can vary by context, and quite is especially variable in British English.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng các từ như 'khá', 'tương đối', 'hơi', 'rất' khá linh hoạt, nên người học dễ chọn sai mức độ khi dịch trực tiếp. Cần chú ý rằng fairly là nhẹ hơn very, còn rather thường hơi mạnh hoặc có sắc thái bất ngờ hơn fairly.

title: Adjective + Preposition
summary: Fixed pairings such as interested in and afraid of, which must be learned as units.

commonMistakes.right: I am interested in learning English.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective interested is normally followed by in, not by other prepositions.
commonMistakes.wrong: I am interested on learning English.

commonMistakes.right: She is afraid of dogs.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective afraid is followed by of. Using about here is not standard in this meaning.
commonMistakes.wrong: She is afraid about dogs.

commonMistakes.right: We are good at maths.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective good is followed by at when we talk about skill or ability.
commonMistakes.wrong: We are good in maths.

commonMistakes.right: He is responsible for the project.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective responsible is followed by for when we mean duty or obligation.
commonMistakes.wrong: He is responsible of the project.

commonMistakes.right: I am excited about the trip.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective excited is usually followed by about when we mean pleased and looking forward to something.
commonMistakes.wrong: I am excited for the trip.

acceptedAnswers: in
interested in
drills.explanation: Interested is normally followed by in. The whole expression is learned as a fixed pair.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: interested ___
drills.target: in

acceptedAnswers: of
afraid of
drills.explanation: Afraid is followed by of. In English, this combination is fixed.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: afraid ___
drills.target: of

acceptedAnswers: at
good at
drills.explanation: Good is followed by at when we describe ability or skill.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: good ___
drills.target: at

acceptedAnswers: for
responsible for
drills.explanation: Responsible is followed by for when it means in charge of or having a duty.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: responsible ___
drills.target: for

acceptedAnswers: of
fond of
drills.explanation: Fond is followed by of when it means liking something or someone.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: fond ___
drills.target: of

acceptedAnswers: on
keen on
drills.explanation: Keen is often followed by on to mean very interested in or enthusiastic about something.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: keen ___
drills.target: on

acceptedAnswers: Choose the correct sentence. I am interested in science.
choices: Choose the correct sentence. I am interested on science.
Choose the correct sentence. I am interested in science.
Choose the correct sentence. I am interested at science.
drills.explanation: Interested is followed by in, so the second sentence is correct.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Choose the correct sentence. I am interested in science.

acceptedAnswers: She is afraid of snakes.
choices: She is afraid about snakes.
She is afraid of snakes.
She is afraid to snakes.
drills.explanation: Afraid is followed by of, not about or to.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She is afraid of snakes.

acceptedAnswers: He is good at tennis.
choices: He is good in tennis.
He is good at tennis.
He is good on tennis.
drills.explanation: Good takes at when we talk about a skill, subject, or activity.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He is good at tennis.

acceptedAnswers: I am excited about the holiday.
choices: I am excited for the holiday.
I am excited about the holiday.
I am excited of the holiday.
drills.explanation: Excited about is the correct pattern when we mean looking forward to something.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I am excited about the holiday.

acceptedAnswers: We are proud of our team.
choices: We are proud for our team.
We are proud of our team.
We are proud to our team.
drills.explanation: Proud is followed by of when we say what causes the feeling.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: We are proud of our team.

acceptedAnswers: I am worried about the exam.
choices: I am worried of the exam.
I am worried about the exam.
I am worried in the exam.
drills.explanation: Worried is commonly followed by about when we talk about concern.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I am worried about the exam.

acceptedAnswers: I am responsible for the budget.
choices: I am responsible of the budget.
I am responsible for the budget.
I am responsible about the budget.
drills.explanation: Responsible is followed by for when we mean having control or duty for something.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I am responsible for the budget.

acceptedAnswers: She is interested in history. He is afraid of heights. They are good at problem-solving.
She is interested in history.
He is afraid of heights.
They are good at problem-solving.
drills.explanation: Each adjective has its own common preposition: interested in, afraid of, good at.
drills.prompt: Write three correct sentences using these adjective-preposition pairs: interested / in, afraid / of, good / at.
drills.target: She is interested in history. He is afraid of heights. They are good at problem-solving.

acceptedAnswers: The manager is responsible for the report.
drills.explanation: Responsible for is the correct fixed pattern. The sentence is complete and natural.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using the adjective + preposition pattern correctly: The manager has duty to the report.
drills.target: The manager is responsible for the report.

acceptedAnswers: I am keen on learning English.
drills.explanation: Keen on means very interested in or enthusiastic about something. The verb form after the preposition can be a gerund.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: I am keen to learning English.
drills.target: I am keen on learning English.

explanation: Many adjectives in English are followed by a specific preposition, and the pair must be memorised together. The preposition is not chosen by a simple logic rule, so Vietnamese learners often transfer the wrong preposition from a similar meaning in Vietnamese. For example, interested in, afraid of, good at, responsible for, fond of, keen on, proud of, worried about, and excited about are common fixed patterns. In IELTS writing and speaking, using the wrong preposition makes the sentence sound unnatural even when the vocabulary is advanced. A useful habit is to learn each adjective together with its preposition and one real example sentence.
explanationVi: Trong tiếng Anh, nhiều tính từ phải đi kèm một giới từ cố định, và cả cụm đó nên học như một đơn vị. Không thể dịch từng từ từ tiếng Việt sang tiếng Anh rồi chọn giới từ theo cảm giác, vì tiếng Anh và tiếng Việt thường không “khớp” nhau về cấu trúc. Ví dụ: interested in, afraid of, good at, responsible for, fond of, keen on, proud of, worried about, excited about đều là các cụm cố định. Người Việt hay bị ảnh hưởng bởi cách diễn đạt tiếng Việt như “quan tâm về”, “sợ về”, “giỏi trong”, “chịu trách nhiệm về”, rồi dùng giới từ sai trong tiếng Anh. Trong IELTS, lỗi này không làm câu hoàn toàn sai nghĩa, nhưng làm câu nghe kém tự nhiên và làm giảm điểm ngôn ngữ. Cách học tốt nhất là ghi nhớ cả cụm: tính từ + giới từ + một câu ví dụ cụ thể, thay vì học riêng tính từ và giới từ.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng cấu trúc khác với tiếng Anh, nên người học hay chọn giới từ theo dịch nghĩa trực tiếp: 'quan tâm về' → interested on/about, 'sợ về' → afraid about, 'giỏi trong' → good in, 'trách nhiệm về' → responsible of. Cần học cả cụm cố định thay vì dịch từng từ.

title: So and Such
summary: Intensifying an adjective versus intensifying a noun phrase.

commonMistakes.right: The movie was so boring that I left early.
commonMistakes.why: Use so before an adjective or adverb, and often with that to show a result.
commonMistakes.wrong: The movie was such boring that I left early.

commonMistakes.right: It was such a boring movie that I left early.
commonMistakes.why: Use such before a noun phrase: such + a/an + adjective + noun.
commonMistakes.wrong: It was so a boring movie that I left early.

commonMistakes.right: She spoke so quietly that nobody heard her.
commonMistakes.why: Use so before an adverb.
commonMistakes.wrong: She spoke such quietly that nobody heard her.

commonMistakes.right: He is such a careful driver that I feel safe with him.
commonMistakes.why: Use such before a noun phrase, not before an adjective alone.
commonMistakes.wrong: He is so a careful driver that I feel safe with him.

acceptedAnswers: so
drills.explanation: Use so before an adjective or adverb.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The soup was ___ hot that I had to wait.
drills.target: so

acceptedAnswers: such
drills.explanation: Use such before a noun phrase.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: It was ___ a difficult exam that many students failed.
drills.target: such

acceptedAnswers: She was so tired that she went to bed early.
drills.explanation: So comes before the adjective tired.
drills.prompt: Write a full sentence using so: she / be / tired / that / she / go to bed early
drills.target: She was so tired that she went to bed early.

acceptedAnswers: It was such a noisy room that I could not hear the teacher.
drills.explanation: Such is used before a noun phrase: such a noisy room.
drills.prompt: Rewrite with such: The room was so noisy that I could not hear the teacher.
drills.target: It was such a noisy room that I could not hear the teacher.

acceptedAnswers: so
drills.explanation: Use so before the adverb quickly.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: He ran ___ quickly that he won the race.
drills.target: so

acceptedAnswers: such
drills.explanation: Use such before a noun phrase with an adjective.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: They are ___ friendly neighbors that we often visit them.
drills.target: such

acceptedAnswers: The test was such a difficult test that nobody finished it.
Choose the correct sentence.
choices: The test was so difficult test that nobody finished it.
The test was such a difficult that nobody finished it.
The test was such a difficult test that nobody finished it.
drills.explanation: Such is followed by a noun phrase, and so is not used before a noun phrase like a difficult test.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The test was such a difficult test that nobody finished it.

acceptedAnswers: The coffee was so strong that I could not sleep.
drills.explanation: So is used before the adjective strong.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: The coffee was such strong that I could not sleep.
drills.target: The coffee was so strong that I could not sleep.

explanation: So is used to intensify an adjective or an adverb: so hot, so quickly. Such is used to intensify a noun phrase: such a hot day, such quick work, such a difficult exam. With so, the result is often shown with that: so tired that... With such, the structure is usually such + (a/an) + adjective + noun: such a good idea, such an interesting book. Be careful: so is not used directly before a noun phrase, and such is not used before an adjective alone.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường dùng một từ nhấn mạnh cho cả tính từ/trạng từ và cụm danh từ. Trong tiếng Anh, phải phân biệt so + tính từ/trạng từ và such + cụm danh từ.

title: Comparative with -er
summary: Short adjectives taking -er than.
explanation:
Short adjectives form the comparative with -er plus than: cheap becomes cheaper than.

Use -er with one-syllable adjectives (tall, fast, cheap) and with two-syllable adjectives ending in -y (happy, easy, busy), where the y becomes i: happier, easier.

Spelling: double a final consonant after a single vowel (big becomes bigger, hot becomes hotter). Longer adjectives take "more" instead - that is a separate point.

"Than" is required whenever you name the thing compared. "She is taller" alone is fine only when the comparison is already obvious from context.
formPatterns: short vowel + consonant: double the consonant + -er

examples.en: This phone is cheaper than mine.
examples.vi: Chiec dien thoai nay re hon cua toi.
Hom nay nong hon hom qua.

examples.en: She looks happier than last year.
examples.vi: Co ay trong vui hon nam ngoai.

examples.en: The test was easier than I expected.
examples.vi: Bai kiem tra de hon toi tuong.

examples.en: He runs faster than his brother.
examples.vi: Anh ay chay nhanh hon em trai.

commonMistakes.wrong: This is more cheap than that.
commonMistakes.right: This is cheaper than that.
commonMistakes.why: One-syllable adjectives take -er, not more.

commonMistakes.wrong: She is more happy than before.
commonMistakes.right: She is happier than before.
commonMistakes.why: Two syllables ending in -y take -er.

commonMistakes.wrong: It is biger than mine.
commonMistakes.right: It is bigger than mine.
commonMistakes.why: Double the final consonant after a single short vowel.

commonMistakes.wrong: He is taller then me.
commonMistakes.right: He is taller than me.
commonMistakes.why: Than compares; then sequences.

cheapest
more cheaper
drills.target: cheaper
acceptedAnswers: cheaper
drills.explanation: Cheap is one syllable, so -er.

more hot
hottest
drills.target: hotter
acceptedAnswers: hotter
drills.explanation: Hot doubles the t before -er.

drills.prompt: Choose: She seems ___ than last year.
choices: happier
more happy
happyer
happiest
drills.target: happier
acceptedAnswers: happier
drills.explanation: Happy ends in -y, so y becomes i plus -er.

drills.prompt: Complete with the comparative of "big": An elephant is ___ than a horse.
drills.target: bigger
acceptedAnswers: bigger
drills.explanation: Double the g after a single short vowel.

drills.prompt: Complete with the comparative of "easy": This exercise is ___ than the last one.
drills.target: easier
acceptedAnswers: easier
drills.explanation: Easy ends in -y, so easier.

drills.prompt: Rewrite as a comparison: "My room is small. Your room is smaller."

Your room is smaller than mine
My room is bigger than your room

drills.prompt: Fix: "This car is more fast than mine."
drills.target: This car is faster than mine
acceptedAnswers: This car is faster than mine
This car is faster than my car
This car is faster than mine is

drills.prompt: Build a comparison using: winter / cold / summer

title: Comparative with More
summary: Longer adjectives taking more than.

commonMistakes.right: This book is more interesting than that one.
commonMistakes.why: Use more with longer adjectives like interesting. Do not say more interestinger.
commonMistakes.wrong: This book is more interestinger than that one.

commonMistakes.right: She is more careful than her brother.
commonMistakes.why: Careful uses more in the comparative. The form more careful is correct, but carefuler is not.
commonMistakes.wrong: She is carefuler than her brother.

commonMistakes.right: My car is more expensive than yours.
commonMistakes.why: Expensive takes more in the comparative. More expensiveer is not correct English.
commonMistakes.wrong: My car is more expensiveer than yours.

acceptedAnswers: more
drills.explanation: Use more before many longer adjectives in the comparative form, such as more interesting or more expensive.
drills.prompt: Complete the comparative: This film is ____ interesting than the last one.

acceptedAnswers: This hotel is more comfortable than that one.

This hotel is comfortable than that one.
drills.explanation: More comfortable is the correct comparative form. Comfortableer is not correct English.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: This hotel is more comfortable than that one.

acceptedAnswers: The exam was more difficult than I expected.
drills.explanation: This sentence uses more with the longer adjective difficult to show comparison.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence using more and difficult to compare the exam with your expectation.
drills.target: The exam was more difficult than I expected.

acceptedAnswers: This picture is more beautiful than that one.
drills.explanation: Beautiful takes more in the comparative form. It is not beautifuler.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using the comparative with more: This picture is beautiful. That one is not as beautiful.
drills.target: This picture is more beautiful than that one.

acceptedAnswers: more
more slowly
drills.explanation: Many adverbs also use more in the comparative form, especially longer ones like slowly.
drills.prompt: Complete the comparative: She walked ____ slowly than I did.
drills.target: more

acceptedAnswers: The new road is more convenient than the old road.
choices: The new road is convenienter than the old road.
The new road is more convenient than the old road.
The new road is convenience than the old road.
drills.explanation: Convenient is a longer adjective, so we use more convenient. Convenienter is wrong.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The new road is more convenient than the old road.

acceptedAnswers: The second task is more important than the first task.

drills.prompt: Write a sentence comparing two tasks with important and more.
drills.target: The second task is more important than the first task.

acceptedAnswers: Her new job is more challenging than her old job.

drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using more: Her old job was less challenging than her new job.
drills.target: Her new job is more challenging than her old job.

explanation: Use more with many longer adjectives and adverbs to make the comparative: more interesting, more careful, more expensive, more slowly. This point contrasts with adjectives that usually add -er, such as small → smaller and fast → faster. Do not add -er to longer adjectives: more interesting, not interestinger.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường dùng thêm -er cho mọi tính từ so sánh, nhưng tiếng Anh không làm vậy với nhiều tính từ dài. Hãy dùng more + tính từ, như more interesting, more beautiful, more difficult.

title: Irregular Comparatives
summary: Better, worse, further, and less.

commonMistakes.right: This book is better than that one.
commonMistakes.why: Better is the comparative form of good. Use than after comparatives to show the second thing.
commonMistakes.wrong: This book is gooder than that one.

commonMistakes.right: His pronunciation is worse than mine.
commonMistakes.why: Worse is the comparative form of bad. Do not use badder in standard English.
commonMistakes.wrong: His pronunciation is badder than mine.

commonMistakes.right: We walked further than we planned.
commonMistakes.why: Further is a comparative meaning greater distance, and it is the standard form in this meaning.
commonMistakes.wrong: We walked more far than we planned.

commonMistakes.right: I need less time to finish this task.
commonMistakes.why: Less is the comparative form used with uncountable nouns and amounts. Do not use fewer with time in this meaning.
commonMistakes.wrong: I need fewer time to finish this task.

acceptedAnswers: better
drills.explanation: Better is the comparative form of good.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: This homework is _____ than yesterday's homework.
drills.target: better

acceptedAnswers: worse
drills.explanation: Worse is the comparative form of bad.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: Today my English is _____ than last week.
drills.target: worse

acceptedAnswers: further
drills.explanation: Further is used for greater distance.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The post office is _____ away than the bank.
drills.target: further

acceptedAnswers: less
drills.explanation: Less is used with amounts and uncountable nouns like time, money, and water.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I have _____ time today than yesterday.

acceptedAnswers: My new phone is better than my old one.

My new phone is better than my old one.

drills.explanation: Better is the correct irregular comparative of good.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: My new phone is better than my old one.

acceptedAnswers: The traffic is worse in the evening.
choices: The traffic is badder in the evening.
The traffic is worse in the evening.
The traffic is more worse in the evening.
drills.explanation: Worse is the correct irregular comparative of bad.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The traffic is worse in the evening.

acceptedAnswers: We need less sugar in this tea.
choices: We need fewer sugar in this tea.
We need less sugar in this tea.
We need little sugar in this tea.
drills.explanation: Less is correct with sugar because sugar is uncountable.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: We need less sugar in this tea.

acceptedAnswers: We walked further to find a taxi.
choices: We walked more far to find a taxi.
We walked further to find a taxi.
We walked farer to find a taxi.
drills.explanation: Further is the correct comparative for distance.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: We walked further to find a taxi.

acceptedAnswers: Her results are better than mine.
The exam was worse than I expected.
We need less noise in the classroom.
They travelled further than we did.
drills.explanation: Each sentence uses the correct irregular comparative: better, worse, less, and further.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using the correct irregular comparative: Her results are good compared with mine.

acceptedAnswers: The weather became worse in the afternoon.
drills.explanation: Worse is the correct comparative of bad in this context.
drills.prompt: Write one sentence. Use: weather / become / worse / afternoon
drills.target: The weather became worse in the afternoon.

explanation: English has a few comparative forms that do not add -er or use more. Good becomes better, bad becomes worse, far becomes further, and little becomes less. Use them in comparative sentences, usually with than.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường cố gắng tạo dạng so sánh bằng cách thêm -er cho mọi tính từ, ví dụ gooder hoặc badder. Cũng dễ nhầm less với fewer, và dùng more far thay cho further.

title: Superlatives
summary: Ranking one item above all others in a set.

commonMistakes.right: This is the biggest house in the street.
commonMistakes.why: Use the superlative -est form for one item at the top of a group. "Bigger" compares two things, so it is wrong here.
commonMistakes.wrong: This is the bigger house in the street.

commonMistakes.right: She is the most careful worker in the team.
commonMistakes.why: Use most + adjective for many longer adjectives. "More careful" compares two things, so it does not rank one person above all others.
commonMistakes.wrong: She is the more careful worker in the team.

commonMistakes.right: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
commonMistakes.why: Superlatives need the full group idea, often with in or of. Without that, the comparison is incomplete.
commonMistakes.wrong: Mount Everest is the highest mountain.

commonMistakes.right: This is the best movie of the year.
commonMistakes.why: Best is the superlative form of good. "Better" is only for comparing two things.
commonMistakes.wrong: This is the better movie of the year.

acceptedAnswers: the tallest
drills.explanation: Use the superlative form to show one person or thing is above all others in the group.
drills.prompt: My brother is ______ in the family.
drills.target: the tallest

acceptedAnswers: This is the cheapest phone in the shop.
drills.explanation: The sentence needs the superlative because it compares one phone with all the others in the shop.
drills.prompt: Make a sentence. Use: this / cheap / phone / in the shop
drills.target: This is the cheapest phone in the shop.

acceptedAnswers: She is the best student in the class.
drills.explanation: Best is the superlative form of good, and it fits when one student is ranked above all the others.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with a superlative: She is better than everyone else in the class.
drills.target: She is the best student in the class.

acceptedAnswers: This building is the tallest one in the city.
choices: This building is the taller one in the city.
This building is the tallest one in the city.
This building is more tall than the city.
drills.explanation: Choose the sentence that uses the superlative to rank one building above all the others in the city.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: This building is the tallest one in the city.

acceptedAnswers: It is the most expensive car in the showroom.
drills.explanation: For longer adjectives like expensive, use most + adjective to make the superlative.
drills.prompt: Make a sentence. Use: it / most expensive / car / in the showroom
drills.target: It is the most expensive car in the showroom.

acceptedAnswers: the most interesting
drills.explanation: Most interesting is the superlative form. It shows one thing stands above the rest in a group.
drills.prompt: This is ______ part of the lesson.
drills.target: the most interesting

acceptedAnswers: He is the oldest player on the team.
drills.explanation: Old becomes oldest in the superlative. Use on the team to show the full group.
drills.prompt: Make a sentence. Use: he / old / player / on the team
drills.target: He is the oldest player on the team.

acceptedAnswers: This is the worst day of my life.
drills.explanation: Worst is the superlative form of bad. It means one day is worse than every other day in the set.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with a superlative: This day is worse than all the others in my life.
drills.target: This is the worst day of my life.

acceptedAnswers: This river is the longest in Vietnam.
choices: This river is longer in Vietnam.
This river is the longest in Vietnam.
This river is the more long in Vietnam.
drills.explanation: The superlative form is longest because one river is ranked above all the others in Vietnam.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: This river is the longest in Vietnam.

explanation: Superlatives show that one person, thing, place, or time is at the top of a group. Use the -est form with short adjectives like tall → tallest, and use most + adjective with longer adjectives like expensive → most expensive. Superlatives are often followed by in or of to show the full group: the tallest in the class, the best of all.
formPatterns: the best / the worst / the most ... + in/of + group
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường quên mạo từ the trước so sánh nhất, hoặc dùng hơn thay vì dạng nhất khi muốn xếp hạng một vật trong cả nhóm.

title: As ... As
summary: Equality and, in the negative, inequality.

commonMistakes.right: My car is as fast as my brother's car.
commonMistakes.why: Use as + adjective + as to show equality.
commonMistakes.wrong: My car is so fast as my brother's car.

commonMistakes.right: This exercise is not as difficult as the last one.
commonMistakes.why: In the negative, English usually uses not as ... as to show less equality.
commonMistakes.wrong: This exercise is not so difficult as the last one.

commonMistakes.right: She is as tall as her mother.
commonMistakes.why: The first as must be followed by an adjective or adverb, then the second as.
commonMistakes.wrong: She is as tall like her mother.

commonMistakes.right: He works as hard as his classmates.
commonMistakes.why: As ... as can compare adverbs or adjectives, but the structure must stay complete.
commonMistakes.wrong: He works as hard his classmates.

acceptedAnswers: My room is as big as yours.
choices: My room is so big as yours.
My room is as big as yours.
My room is as biggest as yours.

drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: My room is as big as yours.

acceptedAnswers: as
This book is not as interesting as that one.
drills.explanation: In the negative, not as ... as is the normal pattern for inequality.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: This book is not ___ interesting ___ that one.
drills.target: as

acceptedAnswers: She is as careful as her teacher.
drills.explanation: The structure is as + adjective + as.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with: she / as careful as / her teacher
drills.target: She is as careful as her teacher.

acceptedAnswers: The blue bag is as expensive as the red bag.
choices: The blue bag is as expensive as the red bag.

The blue bag is as more expensive as the red bag.
drills.explanation: As ... as is used with adjectives to show two things are equal in a quality.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The blue bag is as expensive as the red bag.

acceptedAnswers: as
drills.explanation: The pattern is as + adjective + as.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The exam was ___ easy ___ I expected.
drills.target: as

acceptedAnswers: He can run as fast as his older brother.
drills.explanation: As ... as can also compare adverbs such as fast.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with: he / can run / as fast as / his older brother
drills.target: He can run as fast as his older brother.

acceptedAnswers: The box is not as heavy as the table.
choices: The box is not so heavy as the table.
The box is not as heavy as the table.
The box is no as heavy as the table.
drills.explanation: Not as ... as is the standard form in modern English; the other options are not correct in this structure.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The box is not as heavy as the table.

acceptedAnswers: Her English is as good as mine.

explanation: As ... as is the standard pattern for showing equality in English. Use as + adjective/adverb + as. In negative sentences, English normally uses not as ... as to show that one thing has less of a quality than another.
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt hay dùng 'so ... as' hoặc bỏ một từ so sánh cuối cùng, vì tiếng Việt thường chỉ cần 'bằng' hoặc 'không bằng' mà không cần lặp lại cấu trúc cố định như tiếng Anh.

drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

title: Double Comparative
summary: The more you practise, the better you get.

commonMistakes.right: The more you practise, the better you get.
commonMistakes.why: Double comparatives use one comparative in each clause to show that two changes happen together.
commonMistakes.wrong: The more you practise, better you get.

commonMistakes.right: The harder I study, the more confident I feel.
commonMistakes.why: Each side of the structure needs its own comparative form.
commonMistakes.wrong: The harder I study, more confident I feel.

commonMistakes.right: The sooner we leave, the sooner we will arrive.
commonMistakes.why: In this pattern, both clauses should use parallel comparative forms.
commonMistakes.wrong: The sooner we leave, sooner we will arrive.

commonMistakes.right: The more information you give me, the better I can help.
commonMistakes.why: A double comparative links cause and result with matching comparative forms.
commonMistakes.wrong: The more information you give me, better I can help.

acceptedAnswers: The more you practise, the better you get.
choices: The more you practise, better you get.
The more you practise, the better you get.
More you practise, the better you get.
drills.explanation: This pattern uses the comparative more... the better to show a relationship between two changes.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The more you practise, the better you get.

acceptedAnswers: The harder you work, the more successful you become.

acceptedAnswers: The more we wait, the worse the traffic gets.

acceptedAnswers: The earlier you start, the easier it is to finish on time.
