choices: The teacher asked the students sit down.
The teacher asked the students to sit down.
The teacher asked the students sitting down.
drills.explanation: Ask is followed by object + to-infinitive, not a bare infinitive.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The teacher asked the students to sit down.

acceptedAnswers: She persuaded him to apply for the job.
choices: She persuaded him apply for the job.
She persuaded him to apply for the job.
She persuaded to him apply for the job.
drills.explanation: Persuade needs an object before to + verb: persuaded him to apply.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She persuaded him to apply for the job.

acceptedAnswers: to arrive
We expected them to arrive on time.
drills.explanation: Expect can take an object followed by to + infinitive. The object is them, and the verb after it must be to arrive.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: We expected them ___ on time.
drills.target: to arrive

acceptedAnswers: to explain
I want her to explain the problem.
drills.explanation: The pattern is want + object + to-infinitive. Here, her is the object and to explain is the verb phrase.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I want her ___ the problem.
drills.target: to explain

acceptedAnswers: The boss expects us to finish early.
drills.explanation: Expect is followed by an object plus to-infinitive. English does not use expect us finish.
drills.prompt: Write the sentence using these words: boss / expects / us / finish / early
drills.target: The boss expects us to finish early.

acceptedAnswers: The doctor told me to rest for two days.
drills.explanation: Tell also follows object + to-infinitive: told me to rest. This is different from plain verb + infinitive like want to rest, where no object is needed.
drills.prompt: Write the sentence using these words: doctor / told / me / rest / for two days
drills.target: The doctor told me to rest for two days.

acceptedAnswers: My parents wanted me to study abroad.
drills.explanation: Wanted + object + to-infinitive is the correct pattern. Vietnamese often omits the object-to link, but English needs it.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: My parents wanted me study abroad.
drills.target: My parents wanted me to study abroad.

acceptedAnswers: The manager asked us to leave the room.
drills.explanation: Asked takes object + to-infinitive. The corrected sentence is the full standard pattern.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: The manager asked us leave the room.
drills.target: The manager asked us to leave the room.

acceptedAnswers: I persuaded my brother to join the gym.
choices: I persuaded my brother join the gym.
I persuaded my brother to join the gym.
I persuaded my brother joining the gym.
drills.explanation: Only the sentence with to + verb after the object is correct.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I persuaded my brother to join the gym.

acceptedAnswers: They expected her to win the competition.
drills.explanation: Expected is followed by object + to-infinitive, not a bare infinitive. Here, her is the object and to win is the complement.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using object + to-infinitive: They expected that she would win the competition.
drills.target: They expected her to win the competition.

acceptedAnswers: to leave
She wants to leave early.
drills.explanation: This sentence has only verb + infinitive: wants to leave. There is no object before the infinitive, so it contrasts with want you to leave.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: She wants ___ early.
drills.target: to leave

acceptedAnswers: I told him to call you later.
drills.explanation: Tell + object + to-infinitive is the correct structure. It is not the same as a plain infinitive after tell.
drills.prompt: Write the sentence using these words: I / told / him / call / you / later
drills.target: I told him to call you later.

acceptedAnswers: The company expected the team to work harder.
drills.explanation: Expect uses an object plus to-infinitive. This pattern is common in formal English and IELTS writing.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using object + to-infinitive: The company expected that the team would work harder.
drills.target: The company expected the team to work harder.

explanation: With verbs like want, ask, expect, tell, persuade, and invite, English often uses this pattern: verb + object + to-infinitive. The object is the person who does the action, and to-infinitive shows the action itself: I want you to help, She persuaded him to apply, The teacher asked us to sit down. This is different from plain verb + infinitive, where there is no object between the main verb and to: I want to help, not I want me to help. Vietnamese learners often transfer the Vietnamese pattern too directly and omit to after the object. In English, that is usually wrong.
explanationVi: Trong tiếng Anh, nhiều động từ như want, ask, expect, tell, persuade, invite, encourage, advise, remind thường theo cấu trúc: động từ chính + tân ngữ + to + động từ nguyên mẫu. Tân ngữ là người sẽ thực hiện hành động. Ví dụ: I want you to help me, She persuaded him to apply, The teacher asked us to sit down. Điểm này khác với cấu trúc động từ + to-infinitive đơn thuần, như I want to help, vì ở đó không có tân ngữ chen giữa động từ chính và to-infinitive. Người học tiếng Việt hay bỏ to sau tân ngữ vì trong tiếng Việt có thể diễn đạt gần giống trực tiếp hơn, nhưng trong tiếng Anh cách đó thường sai. Hãy nhớ: nếu có người được tác động làm gì, thường cần object + to + verb.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng cấu trúc đơn giản hơn như “muốn ai làm gì”, “khuyên ai làm gì”, “bảo ai làm gì” mà không có từ tương đương bắt buộc với to. Vì vậy người học dễ bỏ to sau tân ngữ: “I want you help”, “She persuaded him join”. Trong tiếng Anh, phải có object + to + verb.

minimalPairs.meaning: The person himself/herself is the one doing the action.
minimalPairs.sentence: I want to leave early.

minimalPairs.meaning: A different person is being asked or expected to do the action.
minimalPairs.sentence: I want you to leave early.

title: Time Clauses
summary: When, while, until, as soon as, and why a future clause takes the present simple.

commonMistakes.right: I will call you when I arrive.
commonMistakes.why: In time clauses, English uses the present simple after when for a future meaning. Vietnamese often uses a future marker in both clauses, but English does not.
commonMistakes.wrong: I will call you when I will arrive.

commonMistakes.right: Please wait here until the manager comes.
commonMistakes.why: After until, we use the present simple to talk about a future event that completes the time period. The future form is wrong in the time clause.
commonMistakes.wrong: Please wait here until the manager will come.

commonMistakes.right: As soon as the film starts, we will sit down.
commonMistakes.why: After as soon as, English uses the present simple in the time clause, even though the meaning is future. Vietnamese speakers often overuse will here.
commonMistakes.wrong: As soon as the film will start, we will sit down.

commonMistakes.right: While I was cooking, my son was doing homework.
commonMistakes.why: While usually connects two actions happening at the same time. A future form is wrong here because the clause describes a simultaneous past action, not a future plan.
commonMistakes.wrong: While I cooked, my son was doing homework.

acceptedAnswers: when
drills.explanation: Use when to introduce the time clause. In future meaning, the verb in the time clause stays in the present simple.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I will phone you ___ I get home.
drills.target: when

acceptedAnswers: until
drills.explanation: Until is used to show the end point of an action or state.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: We will wait here ___ the rain stops.
drills.target: until

acceptedAnswers: as soon as
drills.explanation: As soon as means immediately after. The time clause takes the present simple, even with future meaning.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I will email you ___ I finish the report.
drills.target: as soon as

acceptedAnswers: while
drills.explanation: While is used for two actions happening at the same time.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: ___ I was studying, my brother was watching TV.
drills.target: while

acceptedAnswers: I will call you when I arrive.
choices: I will call you when I arrive.
I will call you when I will arrive.
I call you when I will arrive.
drills.explanation: In a future time clause after when, English uses the present simple, not will.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

acceptedAnswers: Please wait here until the manager comes.
choices: Please wait here until the manager will come.
Please wait here until the manager comes.

drills.explanation: After until, the time clause takes the present simple. Will is not used in the time clause.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Please wait here until the manager comes.

acceptedAnswers: As soon as the film starts, we will sit down.
choices: As soon as the film will start, we will sit down.
As soon as the film starts, we will sit down.
As soon as the film starting, we will sit down.
drills.explanation: As soon as introduces a future time clause, so the verb is in the present simple.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: As soon as the film starts, we will sit down.

acceptedAnswers: While I was cooking, my son was doing homework.
choices: While I cooked, my son was doing homework.
While I was cooking, my son was doing homework.
While I was cook, my son was doing homework.
drills.explanation: While connects actions happening at the same time. The progressive form fits the ongoing actions in the past.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: While I was cooking, my son was doing homework.

acceptedAnswers: until
drills.explanation: Until means up to a point in time.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: Don’t leave ___ I finish speaking.
drills.target: until

acceptedAnswers: when
drills.explanation: When can refer to a future time in the time clause, but the verb stays in the present simple.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: Call me ___ you are ready.
drills.target: when

acceptedAnswers: I will stay here until you come back.
drills.explanation: The future meaning is in the main clause. The until-clause uses the present simple.
drills.prompt: Write one correct sentence using until and the idea: stay here / you come back / future meaning.
drills.target: I will stay here until you come back.

acceptedAnswers: As soon as I get the message, I will reply.
drills.explanation: As soon as introduces a time clause, so get is in the present simple even though the meaning is future.
drills.prompt: Write one correct sentence using as soon as and the idea: get the message / reply / future meaning.
drills.target: As soon as I get the message, I will reply.

acceptedAnswers: When I finish work, I will call my mother.
drills.explanation: In the when-clause, finish is in the present simple. The future form belongs in the main clause.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence correctly: When I will finish work, I will call my mother.
drills.target: When I finish work, I will call my mother.

acceptedAnswers: I will not leave until she arrives.
drills.explanation: After until, the verb in the time clause is present simple. The negative future idea is expressed in the main clause.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence correctly: I will not leave until she will arrive.
drills.target: I will not leave until she arrives.

acceptedAnswers: When the meeting starts, please turn off your phone.
drills.explanation: A future time clause after when uses the present simple. Please keep the imperative in the main clause.
drills.prompt: Write one correct sentence using when and the idea: meeting starts / turn off your phone / future meaning.
drills.target: When the meeting starts, please turn off your phone.

explanation: Time clauses are clauses that tell us when something happens: when, while, until, as soon as, before, and after. The key rule for IELTS learners is this: in a time clause, English normally uses the present simple to talk about the future, not will. So we say I will call you when I arrive, not when I will arrive; Please wait until the manager comes, not until the manager will come; and As soon as I finish, I will leave. The future meaning is shown by the main clause, while the time clause stays in the present simple. Use while for actions happening at the same time, often with past continuous forms when describing an ongoing past action. If you are talking about an event that is still in progress or repeated, the present simple or present continuous may also appear in the time clause depending on meaning, but will is not used there for future time.
explanationVi: Mệnh đề chỉ thời gian là mệnh đề nói về thời điểm một việc xảy ra, thường có when, while, until, as soon as, before, after. Điểm rất quan trọng là: trong mệnh đề thời gian, tiếng Anh thường dùng thì hiện tại đơn để nói về tương lai, không dùng will. Vì vậy ta nói I will call you when I arrive, không nói when I will arrive; Please wait until the manager comes, không nói until the manager will come; As soon as I finish, I will leave. Ý nghĩa tương lai nằm ở mệnh đề chính, còn mệnh đề thời gian vẫn dùng hiện tại đơn. While dùng cho hai hành động xảy ra cùng lúc, và khi kể về quá khứ đang diễn ra thì thường dùng quá khứ tiếp diễn. Người Việt hay bị ảnh hưởng bởi cách nói tiếng Việt là cả hai mệnh đề đều có thể mang ý tương lai, nên rất dễ viết will trong mệnh đề when/as soon as/until. Cần nhớ: nếu là mệnh đề thời gian nói về tương lai, hãy dùng hiện tại đơn trong mệnh đề đó.
formPatterns: as soon as + present simple, main clause + future
while + past continuous, main clause + past continuous
when/after/before/as soon as/until + present simple in future time clauses
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không bắt buộc đổi động từ trong mệnh đề thời gian khi nói về tương lai, nên người học dễ thêm will vào cả hai mệnh đề. Cần nhắc rõ: trong tiếng Anh, mệnh đề sau when/as soon as/until/before/after thường dùng hiện tại đơn nếu câu mang nghĩa tương lai.

title: Purpose Clauses
summary: So that and in order that, where a clause rather than an infinitive expresses purpose.

commonMistakes.right: I left early so that I could catch the last bus.
commonMistakes.why: Use so that + clause when you need a subject and a verb after the purpose connector.
commonMistakes.wrong: I left early so that catch the last bus.

commonMistakes.right: She spoke slowly in order that everyone could understand her.
commonMistakes.why: In order that is followed by a clause, not by a bare verb form.
commonMistakes.wrong: She spoke slowly in order that everyone understand her.

commonMistakes.right: We turned off the lights so that the baby could sleep.
commonMistakes.why: A purpose clause needs a finite verb such as could sleep; a bare infinitive does not follow so that.
commonMistakes.wrong: We turned off the lights so that the baby sleep.

acceptedAnswers: so that
drills.explanation: So that introduces a purpose clause with a subject and verb.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I turned down the music _____ my neighbors could sleep.
drills.target: so that

acceptedAnswers: in order that
drills.explanation: In order that is a formal purpose connector followed by a clause.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: The speaker paused _____ the audience could take notes.
drills.target: in order that

acceptedAnswers: I saved the document so that I would not lose my work.
drills.explanation: So that is used here because the purpose is expressed as a clause with its own subject and verb.
drills.prompt: Write one sentence. Use so that to show purpose: I saved the document / I would not lose my work.
drills.target: I saved the document so that I would not lose my work.

acceptedAnswers: She arrived early in order that she could find a seat.
drills.explanation: In order that is followed by a full clause, often in formal writing.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using in order that: She arrived early to find a seat.
drills.target: She arrived early in order that she could find a seat.

acceptedAnswers: We speak clearly so that students can follow the lesson.
drills.explanation: A purpose clause uses a finite verb after so that, not an infinitive.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: We speak clearly so that students to follow the lesson.
drills.target: We speak clearly so that students can follow the lesson.

acceptedAnswers: I explained the rule in order that nobody would be confused.
choices: I explained the rule in order that nobody would be confused.
I explained the rule in order to nobody would be confused.
I explained the rule so that nobody would be confused to.
drills.explanation: The correct sentence uses in order that + clause. The other options are ungrammatical.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I explained the rule in order that nobody would be confused.

acceptedAnswers: so that
drills.explanation: So that is the connector for a purpose clause here; the infinitive of purpose would be a different structure.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: She set an alarm _____ she would wake up on time.
drills.target: so that

acceptedAnswers: We moved the meeting earlier in order that more people could attend.
drills.explanation: This sentence shows purpose with a clause after in order that, which is especially common in formal English.
drills.prompt: Write one sentence. Use in order that to show purpose: We moved the meeting earlier / more people could attend.
drills.target: We moved the meeting earlier in order that more people could attend.

acceptedAnswers: He spoke loudly so that the people at the back could hear him.
drills.explanation: So that is correct because the purpose is stated in a clause, not with an infinitive.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using so that: He spoke loudly to be heard by the people at the back.
drills.target: He spoke loudly so that the people at the back could hear him.

explanation: Purpose clauses use so that and in order that when the purpose is expressed with a full clause containing a subject and a finite verb. This is different from the infinitive of purpose, such as to catch the bus or to find a seat, where no subject is stated in the purpose phrase. So that is common in speech and writing; in order that is more formal and less frequent. After these connectors, the verb is often in a modal clause such as could, would, or can, depending on time and meaning.
formPatterns: main clause + so that + subject + modal verb + base verb
main clause + in order that + subject + modal verb + base verb
Purpose clauses are different from infinitive-of-purpose structures like to + verb
l1Notes: Người học tiếng Việt thường dùng động từ nguyên mẫu sau so that/in order that, nhưng tiếng Anh cần mệnh đề có chủ ngữ và động từ hữu hạn.

minimalPairs.meaning: Purpose with a clause: the action is done to achieve a result.
minimalPairs.sentence: I left early so that I could catch the last bus.

minimalPairs.meaning: Purpose with an infinitive: the action is done to achieve a result, but the purpose phrase uses to + verb.
minimalPairs.sentence: I left early to catch the last bus.

minimalPairs.meaning: Purpose with a clause: the speaker explains why the lights were turned off.
minimalPairs.sentence: We turned off the lights so that the baby could sleep.

minimalPairs.meaning: Purpose with an infinitive: the speaker explains why the lights were turned off, using to + verb.
minimalPairs.sentence: We turned off the lights to let the baby sleep.

title: Mandative Subjunctive
summary: The bare form after suggest, recommend, insist and demand: I suggest that he go.

commonMistakes.right: I suggest that he go now.
commonMistakes.why: After suggest, we often use mandative subjunctive in formal English: base verb form after that. In standard British and American English, he goes is not the same structure here.
commonMistakes.wrong: I suggest that he goes now.

commonMistakes.right: The teacher insisted that she be on time.
commonMistakes.why: After insist in this structure, the verb stays in the base form: be, not is/was.
commonMistakes.wrong: The teacher insisted that she is on time.

commonMistakes.right: We recommended that the report be revised.
commonMistakes.why: After recommend, the mandative subjunctive uses the base verb form be, not was or is.
commonMistakes.wrong: We recommended that the report was revised.

commonMistakes.right: The committee demanded that he leave immediately.
commonMistakes.why: After demand, the verb is in base form: leave. Adding -s is incorrect in this construction.
commonMistakes.wrong: The committee demanded that he leaves immediately.

acceptedAnswers: I suggest that he go to the doctor.
choices: I suggest that he goes to the doctor.
I suggest that he go to the doctor.
I suggest that he went to the doctor.
drills.explanation: After suggest, the mandative subjunctive uses the base form of the verb: go. The third-person -s form is not used in this structure.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I suggest that he go to the doctor.

acceptedAnswers: that the meeting start at 9 a.m.
drills.explanation: After recommend in this structure, the verb stays in the base form: start. The word that introduces the clause, and the verb does not take -s.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: We recommend ______ at 9 a.m.
drills.target: that the meeting start at 9 a.m.

acceptedAnswers: The doctor insisted that the patient be admitted immediately.
drills.explanation: In the mandative subjunctive, insist is followed by that + subject + base verb. Be stays be here; it does not change to is or was.
drills.prompt: Write a full sentence using: insist / patient / be admitted / immediately
drills.target: The doctor insisted that the patient be admitted immediately.

acceptedAnswers: The manager demanded that he leave at once.
drills.explanation: Demand can take the mandative subjunctive in formal English. After that, use the base verb leave, not leaves.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence in the mandative subjunctive form: The manager demanded his leaving at once.
drills.target: The manager demanded that he leave at once.

acceptedAnswers: The law requires that every driver wear a seat belt.
choices: The law requires that every driver wear a seat belt.
The law requires that every driver wears a seat belt.
The law requires that every driver wore a seat belt.
drills.explanation: This is another mandative subjunctive pattern: require + that + subject + base verb. Wear is correct here; wears is not.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The law requires that every driver wear a seat belt.

acceptedAnswers: It is essential that she arrive early.
drills.explanation: After adjectives like essential, important, necessary, the mandative subjunctive uses the base verb arrive. This is a formal recommendation or requirement, not a past-time meaning.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: It is essential that she arrives early.
drills.target: It is essential that she arrive early.

acceptedAnswers: The board insisted that the accounts be checked twice.
drills.explanation: Insist is followed by that + subject + base verb in this construction. Be is the base form, and the passive structure be checked is correct.
drills.prompt: Write a full sentence: board / insist / accounts / be checked twice
drills.target: The board insisted that the accounts be checked twice.

acceptedAnswers: He demanded that I not tell anyone.
choices: He demanded that I not tell anyone.
He demanded that I didn't tell anyone.
He demanded that I don't tell anyone.
drills.explanation: In the mandative subjunctive, not comes before the base verb: not tell. Do not use didn't or don't in this structure.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: He demanded that I not tell anyone.

acceptedAnswers: I insist that she study harder.
drills.explanation: After insist, the verb study stays in the base form. This is a demand or strong recommendation, not a real present-tense statement about her habit.
drills.prompt: Rewrite using the mandative subjunctive: I insist on her studying harder.
drills.target: I insist that she study harder.

explanation:
The mandative subjunctive is used after verbs and expressions of demand, suggestion, recommendation, necessity, and importance, especially in formal English. The pattern is usually that + subject + base verb: I suggest that he go, We recommended that the report be revised, The teacher insisted that she be on time. The verb after that does not take -s, and it does not change to past form just because the main verb is in the past.

This is different from the subjunctive were. With were, we use were for unreal or hypothetical situations: If I were you, I would study more. That form is about imagined or contrary-to-fact situations. The mandative subjunctive is about obligation, recommendation, or demand: I suggest that he go. Vietnamese learners often add -s after the third person or use was/were by mistake because Vietnamese does not mark this pattern in the same way.
explanationVi:
Mệnh đề giả định sau các động từ như suggest, recommend, insist, demand, require, và sau các tính từ như essential, important, necessary thường dùng cấu trúc that + chủ ngữ + động từ nguyên mẫu không to. Ví dụ: I suggest that he go. The teacher insisted that she be on time. Đây là kiểu câu trang trọng trong tiếng Anh viết và nói học thuật.

Điểm dễ sai là thêm -s vào động từ với ngôi thứ ba số ít, ví dụ he goes, she arrives. Trong cấu trúc này, động từ phải ở dạng nguyên mẫu: he go, she arrive, it be. Cũng không dùng was/were theo nghĩa quá khứ như trong câu tường thuật thông thường. Quá khứ của động từ chính không làm đổi cấu trúc này. Ví dụ: She recommended that the report be revised. Không nói: the report was revised ở đây nếu ý là mệnh lệnh/đề nghị.

Cần phân biệt với subjunctive were. Were dùng cho tình huống giả định, không có thật, hoặc trái với thực tế: If I were you, I would apologize. Còn mandative subjunctive dùng sau động từ/tính từ thể hiện yêu cầu, đề nghị, hoặc sự cần thiết: We insisted that he stay. Hai cấu trúc này đều có tính trang trọng, nhưng ý nghĩa khác nhau: một bên là giả định, một bên là yêu cầu/đề nghị.
formPatterns: It is essential/important/necessary + that + subject + base verb
subject + insist/demand/recommend + that + subject + not + base verb
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường không có cấu trúc tương đương trực tiếp với mandative subjunctive, nên người học hay thêm -s theo thói quen ngữ pháp hiện tại đơn: he goes, she arrives. Một lỗi khác là dùng was/were theo kiểu “quá khứ” hoặc theo ảnh hưởng của câu giả định, trong khi ở đây tiếng Anh dùng động từ nguyên mẫu sau that. Hãy nhớ đây là mẫu diễn đạt yêu cầu/đề nghị/trang trọng: đề nghị rằng anh ấy đi, yêu cầu rằng báo cáo được sửa.

minimalPairs.meaning: Tình huống giả định, trái với thực tế hiện tại.
minimalPairs.sentence: If I were you, I would take the job.

minimalPairs.meaning: Lời đề nghị hoặc yêu cầu trong mệnh đề that.
minimalPairs.sentence: I suggest that you take the job.

title: Of-Genitive Versus Possessive S
summary: When English prefers the roof of the house and when it prefers my brother's car.

commonMistakes.right: My brother's car is in the garage.
commonMistakes.why: Use possessive 's for people and other living owners in normal English.
commonMistakes.wrong: The car of my brother is in the garage.

commonMistakes.right: The roof of the house needs repair.
commonMistakes.why: Use of-genitive for many things, parts, and more formal noun phrases.
commonMistakes.wrong: The house's roof needs repair.

commonMistakes.right: The company's office is in Hanoi.
commonMistakes.why: A company is an organization, so possessive 's is normal here.
commonMistakes.wrong: The office of the company is in Hanoi.

commonMistakes.right: The door of the room is open.
commonMistakes.why: For parts of objects or buildings, English usually prefers of-genitive in this kind of structure.
commonMistakes.wrong: The room's door is open.

acceptedAnswers: My brother's car
drills.explanation: For a person who owns something, English usually uses possessive 's.
drills.prompt: Complete the phrase: My brother ___ car
drills.target: My brother's car

acceptedAnswers: The roof of the house is old.
choices: The roof of the house is old.
The house's roof is old.
The roof from the house is old.
drills.explanation: For a part of a building, of-genitive is natural here.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The roof of the house is old.

acceptedAnswers: My sister's phone is new.
drills.explanation: For a person owner, possessive 's is the normal form.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with: my sister / phone / new
drills.target: My sister's phone is new.

acceptedAnswers: The top of the mountain is covered in snow.
drills.explanation: For a part of a place or thing, of-genitive is common.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with: the top / the mountain / covered in snow
drills.target: The top of the mountain is covered in snow.

acceptedAnswers: The girl's bag was on the chair.
drills.explanation: A child is a person, so possessive 's is appropriate.
drills.prompt: Rewrite with possessive 's: The bag of the girl was on the chair.
drills.target: The girl's bag was on the chair.

acceptedAnswers: The keys of the car were on the table.
drills.explanation: Here of-genitive is possible, but it sounds less natural than the possessive form for a car. This drill practices the noun phrase form itself.
drills.prompt: Rewrite with of-genitive: The car's keys were on the table.
drills.target: The keys of the car were on the table.

acceptedAnswers: The head of the table is missing a screw.
choices: The table's head is missing a screw.
The head of the table is missing a screw.
The head from the table is missing a screw.
drills.explanation: For a part of an object or thing, of-genitive is the natural choice.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The head of the table is missing a screw.

acceptedAnswers: My friend's house is near the river.
drills.explanation: For a friend, possessive 's is the standard form.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: My friend house is near the river.
drills.target: My friend's house is near the river.

acceptedAnswers: The color of the car is red.
choices: The car's color is red.
The color of the car is red.
The color from the car is red.
drills.explanation: Both forms can be correct, but of-genitive is a natural way to name a property of a thing.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The color of the car is red.

acceptedAnswers: The company's profits increased.
The profits of the company increased.
drills.explanation: Both forms are correct in English. Possessive 's is often more direct; of-genitive is also possible.
drills.prompt: Rewrite using possessive 's: The profits of the company increased.
drills.target: The company's profits increased.

acceptedAnswers: The window of the room is broken.
drills.explanation: For a part of a room or building, of-genitive is a safe and natural pattern.
drills.prompt: Write a sentence with: the window / the room / broken
drills.target: The window of the room is broken.

acceptedAnswers: My mother's friend lives here.
drills.explanation: For people, possessive 's is the normal form, even in longer noun phrases.
drills.prompt: Correct the sentence: The friend of my mother lives here.
drills.target: My mother's friend lives here.

acceptedAnswers: The name of the book is interesting.
choices: The book's name is interesting.
The name of the book is interesting.
The name from the book is interesting.
drills.explanation: For a thing like a book, of-genitive is very common, especially in formal or neutral style.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: The name of the book is interesting.

acceptedAnswers: The teacher's desk is near the door.
drills.explanation: For a person who owns or uses something, possessive 's is standard.
drills.prompt: Rewrite with possessive 's: The desk of the teacher is near the door.
drills.target: The teacher's desk is near the door.

explanation: In English, possessive 's and of-genitive both show relationship or ownership, but they are not used in the same way. Possessive 's is common with people and living beings: my brother's car, the teacher's desk, my mother's friend. Of-genitive is common with things, parts of things, and more formal noun phrases: the roof of the house, the window of the room, the name of the book. In many cases, both forms are possible, but one sounds more natural. For example, the company's profits and the profits of the company are both correct, but English often prefers possessive 's for people and organizations, and of-genitive for parts and descriptions of things. Vietnamese often uses one structure like của for both meanings, so learners may overuse of in English or put 's after inanimate nouns too often.
explanationVi: Trong tiếng Anh, possessive 's và cấu trúc of-genitive đều dùng để chỉ quan hệ sở hữu, liên quan, hoặc một phần của cái gì đó, nhưng cách dùng không giống nhau. Possessive 's thường dùng với người và sinh vật: my brother's car, the teacher's desk, my mother's friend. Of-genitive thường dùng với sự vật, bộ phận của vật, hoặc cụm danh từ mang tính trang trọng/trung tính: the roof of the house, the window of the room, the name of the book. Có nhiều trường hợp cả hai đều đúng, nhưng một cách nghe tự nhiên hơn. Ví dụ, the company's profits và the profits of the company đều đúng, nhưng tiếng Anh thường thích possessive 's với người và tổ chức, còn of-genitive với bộ phận và mô tả của sự vật. Người Việt hay dùng một từ “của” cho nhiều kiểu quan hệ, nên dễ viết quá nhiều cấu trúc of trong tiếng Anh hoặc đặt 's không tự nhiên với danh từ không phải người.
formPatterns: For things/parts: the roof of the house
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường dùng “của” cho cả sở hữu, quan hệ và bộ phận, nên người học dễ dịch thẳng thành of trong mọi trường hợp. Cần nhớ: với người/chủ thể sống, tiếng Anh thường ưu tiên possessive 's; với sự vật, bộ phận, hoặc cụm danh từ dài/trang trọng, tiếng Anh часто ưu tiên of-genitive.

minimalPairs.meaning: Căn nhà có phần mái được nói đến bằng cấu trúc of.
minimalPairs.sentence: The roof of the house is red.

minimalPairs.meaning: Phần mái được nói bằng possessive 's; câu này tự nhiên hơn với người học khi muốn nói về mái của một ngôi nhà, nhưng trong bài này nhấn mạnh lựa chọn giữa hai cấu trúc.
minimalPairs.sentence: The house's roof is red.

minimalPairs.meaning: Đây là cụm sở hữu với người sở hữu là bố tôi.
minimalPairs.sentence: My father's car is new.

minimalPairs.meaning: Đây là cụm of-genitive nói về chiếc xe thuộc về bố tôi; vẫn đúng nhưng thường kém tự nhiên hơn trong giao tiếp hằng ngày.
minimalPairs.sentence: The car of my father is new.

title: So Do I And Neither Do I
summary: Agreeing with an auxiliary echo: So do I, Neither did he, I do too.

commonMistakes.right: I like coffee, and so does my sister.
commonMistakes.why: Use so + auxiliary + subject to agree with a positive statement. We do not say 'So my sister does' in this meaning.
commonMistakes.wrong: I like coffee, and so my sister does.

commonMistakes.right: I do not like coffee, and neither does my sister.
commonMistakes.why: Use neither + auxiliary + subject to agree with a negative statement. We do not say 'Neither my sister does' in this meaning.
commonMistakes.wrong: I do not like coffee, and neither my sister does.

commonMistakes.right: She can swim, and so can I.
commonMistakes.why: The auxiliary comes before the subject in this pattern. We do not say 'So I can' here.
commonMistakes.wrong: She can swim, and so I can.

commonMistakes.right: He does not drive, and neither do I.
commonMistakes.why: After neither, English uses inversion: neither + auxiliary + subject. We do not say 'Neither I do' here.
commonMistakes.wrong: He does not drive, and neither I do.

acceptedAnswers: So do I.
choices: So do I.
So I do.
So am I.
drills.explanation: So do I is used to agree with a positive statement when the verb is in the present simple and the auxiliary do is needed.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct agreement sentence.
drills.target: So do I.

acceptedAnswers: Neither do I.
choices: Neither do I.
Neither I do.
So do I.
drills.explanation: Neither do I is used to agree with a negative statement in the present simple.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct agreement sentence.
drills.target: Neither do I.

acceptedAnswers: I do too.
choices: I do too.
I too do.
I do also.
drills.explanation: I do too is a correct alternative way to agree with a positive statement. It is different from the inverted so/neither pattern.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: I do too.

acceptedAnswers: Neither has she.
choices: Neither has she.
Neither she has.
Neither she have.
drills.explanation: After neither, the auxiliary comes before the subject. Here the auxiliary is has, so the correct structure is neither has she.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Neither has she.

acceptedAnswers: So am I.
choices: So am I.
So I am.
So I do.
drills.explanation: Use so + auxiliary + subject to agree with a statement that uses be. The auxiliary here is am.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: So am I.

acceptedAnswers: I like tea, and so does my husband.
drills.explanation: The second clause agrees with the first using so + auxiliary + subject. Because the first verb is like, the auxiliary is does.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence: I like tea / my husband too
drills.target: I like tea, and so does my husband.

acceptedAnswers: I did not go, and neither did my friends.
drills.explanation: The first clause is negative, so the agreeing clause uses neither + auxiliary + subject. In the past simple, the auxiliary is did.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence: I did not go / my friends too
drills.target: I did not go, and neither did my friends.

acceptedAnswers: She can sing, and so can I.
choices: She can sing, and so can I.
She can sing, and so I can.
She can sing, and I can too.
drills.explanation: So can I is the correct inversion pattern after a positive clause with can. The auxiliary can comes before the subject I.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: She can sing, and so can I.

acceptedAnswers: I have finished, and so has he.
drills.explanation: With present perfect, the auxiliary is have/has. The agreement structure is so + auxiliary + subject, so the correct sentence is so has he.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence: I have finished / he too
drills.target: I have finished, and so has he.

acceptedAnswers: She does not smoke, and neither do I.
drills.explanation: A negative statement is followed by neither + auxiliary + subject. The auxiliary agrees with the original verb smoke, so the correct form is do I.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence: She does not smoke / I too
drills.target: She does not smoke, and neither do I.

acceptedAnswers: I am tired, and so is my brother.
drills.explanation: When the first clause uses be, the agreement clause also uses be. The correct inversion is so is my brother.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence: I am tired / my brother too
drills.target: I am tired, and so is my brother.

acceptedAnswers: Neither did he.
drills.explanation: This is the full inverted pattern for agreeing with a negative past statement. Neither is followed by the auxiliary did, then the subject he.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: She did not call, and ______ he.
drills.target: Neither did he.

acceptedAnswers: So do I.
drills.explanation: This fixed agreement phrase uses so + auxiliary + subject. For the present simple with do, the full answer is So do I.
drills.prompt: Complete the sentence: I like pizza. ______
drills.target: So do I.

acceptedAnswers: I like coffee too.
drills.explanation: This is the non-inverted alternative with too. It means the same general agreement as so do I, but the structure is different.
drills.prompt: Rewrite with too: I like coffee, and so does my friend.
drills.target: I like coffee too.

acceptedAnswers: Neither can we.
choices: Neither can we.
So can we.
We can neither.
drills.explanation: Neither can we is the correct inverted agreement after a negative statement. The auxiliary can comes before we.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Neither can we.

explanation:
When you agree with a statement in English, you often repeat only the auxiliary verb, not the main verb. After a positive sentence, use so + auxiliary + subject: I am tired. So am I. She can drive. So can I. After a negative sentence, use neither + auxiliary + subject: I do not like it. Neither do I. He has not arrived. Neither has she.

This pattern is called subject-auxiliary inversion because the auxiliary moves before the subject. It is not the same as the inversion in so/such expressions like So beautiful was the view that we stopped walking, or Such was the noise that I could not sleep. In this lesson, so/ neither do not introduce a degree or result clause; they simply show agreement.

If the verb in the first sentence is present simple, use do/does. If it is past simple, use did. If it uses be, use am/is/are/was/were. If it uses a modal, repeat the modal: can, should, must, and so on. An easy alternative to so + auxiliary + subject is subject + auxiliary + too: I like tea too.
explanationVi:
Trong tiếng Anh, khi muốn “đồng ý” với một câu trước đó, ta thường không lặp lại cả động từ chính mà chỉ lặp lại trợ động từ. Với câu khẳng định, dùng so + trợ động từ + chủ ngữ: I like coffee. So do I. / She can swim. So can I. Với câu phủ định, dùng neither + trợ động từ + chủ ngữ: I do not like coffee. Neither do I. / He has not finished. Neither has he.

Đây là hiện tượng đảo trợ động từ và chủ ngữ: trợ động từ đứng trước chủ ngữ. Nó khác với kiểu đảo trong so/such khi so/such mang nghĩa “quá, đến mức” hoặc mở đầu mệnh đề kết quả, ví dụ: So beautiful was the view that we stopped. Trong bài này, so và neither không mang nghĩa “quá” mà chỉ dùng để đáp lại, đồng ý với câu trước.

Một điểm dễ nhầm với người Việt là tiếng Việt thường chỉ nói rất tự nhiên kiểu “Tôi cũng vậy”, “Tôi cũng không”, không có trợ động từ để đảo. Vì vậy khi sang tiếng Anh phải nhìn động từ của câu trước để chọn đúng trợ động từ: am/is/are, do/does, did, can, has/have, will, should… rồi đảo nó lên trước chủ ngữ. Ngoài ra, bạn cũng có thể nói I do too / I am too / I can too trong một số trường hợp, nhưng so/neither + trợ động từ + chủ ngữ là mẫu chuẩn rất hay gặp trong IELTS.
formPatterns: auxiliary agrees with the verb tense or modal in the first clause
l1Notes: Người Việt hay dịch từng từ kiểu “Tôi cũng vậy” nên viết sai trật tự: đặt chủ ngữ trước trợ động từ hoặc dùng nhầm so/neither với nghĩa của so/such. Hãy nhớ tiếng Anh cần đảo trợ động từ: So do I, Neither can she, So was he. Sau câu phủ định, không dùng too để đồng ý phủ định; dùng neither + trợ động từ + chủ ngữ.

minimalPairs.meaning: Câu này là cách đồng ý với một câu khẳng định trước đó bằng đảo trợ động từ.
minimalPairs.sentence: I like tea. So do I.

minimalPairs.meaning: Câu này là cách nói thêm ý “cũng vậy” không cần đảo trợ động từ.
minimalPairs.sentence: I like tea too.

minimalPairs.meaning: Câu này là cách đồng ý với một câu phủ định trước đó bằng đảo trợ động từ.
minimalPairs.sentence: I do not like tea. Neither do I.

minimalPairs.meaning: Câu này là cách diễn đạt phủ định riêng của người nói, không phải mẫu đồng ý with neither.
minimalPairs.sentence: I do not like tea either.

title: Adverbial Participle Clauses
summary: Having finished the work, she left - compressing a time or reason clause into a participle.

commonMistakes.right: Having finished the work, she left early.
commonMistakes.why: This participle clause shows that she finished the work before she left. It cannot be replaced by a full relative-clause structure like 'who finished the work' because this is about time, not a noun phrase.
commonMistakes.wrong: Finished the work, she left early.

commonMistakes.right: After she had finished the work, she left early.
commonMistakes.why: This is a full time clause with a subject and verb. A bare participle clause is shorter and more compressed, but the full clause is the normal alternative.
commonMistakes.wrong: After finishing the work, she left early.

commonMistakes.right: Feeling tired, he went to bed early.
commonMistakes.why: The participle clause gives the reason or background state for the main action. It is not a reduced relative clause, because it does not modify a noun.
commonMistakes.wrong: Feeling tired, who went to bed early.

commonMistakes.right: Driving home, I saw an accident.
commonMistakes.why: Here the participle clause describes an action happening at the same time as the main verb. It is not a full time clause with 'while' or 'as', though those are possible alternatives.
commonMistakes.wrong: Driving home, while I saw an accident.

acceptedAnswers: Having finished the work, she left early.
choices: Having finished the work, she left early.
Having finished the work, she was left early.
Finished the work, she left early.
drills.explanation: The participle clause 'Having finished the work' compresses the idea that the finishing happened before the leaving. The other options are ungrammatical or change the meaning.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Having finished the work, she left early.

acceptedAnswers: Feeling tired, he went to bed early.
drills.explanation: This is a correct adverbial participle clause. It gives the reason or background state for the main action.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence using the cue: feeling tired / go to bed early / he
drills.target: Feeling tired, he went to bed early.

acceptedAnswers: After finishing the report, I sent it to my manager.
drills.explanation: The participle clause compresses a time relation. It means the report was finished before it was sent.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence using a participle clause: After I finished the report, I sent it to my manager.
drills.target: After finishing the report, I sent it to my manager.

acceptedAnswers: Walking through the park, we saw many birds.
choices: Walking through the park, we saw many birds.
Walking through the park, the birds saw us.
Walked through the park, we saw many birds.
drills.explanation: The participle clause shows the action happening at the same time as the main event. The subject of the participle clause must match the subject of the main clause.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Walking through the park, we saw many birds.

acceptedAnswers: Closing the window, she noticed the rain had stopped.
drills.explanation: This participle clause gives a background action happening just before the main verb. It is shorter than a full time clause like 'When she closed the window...'.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence using the cue: close the window / notice the rain had stopped / she
drills.target: Closing the window, she noticed the rain had stopped.

acceptedAnswers: After he had checked the answers, he submitted the test.
drills.explanation: This is the full time-clause version. It is grammatical, but it is not a participle clause, so it is useful for contrast.
drills.prompt: Rewrite the sentence without a participle clause: Having checked the answers, he submitted the test.
drills.target: After he had checked the answers, he submitted the test.

acceptedAnswers: The boy standing near the door is my cousin.
choices: The boy standing near the door is my cousin.
The boy is standing near the door is my cousin.
Standing near the door is my cousin.
drills.explanation: This is not an adverbial participle clause. Here 'standing near the door' is a reduced relative clause describing 'the boy'.
drills.prompt: Choose the sentence that uses a reduced relative clause, not an adverbial participle clause.
drills.target: The boy standing near the door is my cousin.

acceptedAnswers: Surprised by the results, she called her friend immediately.
drills.explanation: The participle clause describes her emotional state and explains why she called immediately. The clause is adverbial, not a relative clause.
drills.prompt: Build a sentence using the cue: surprise by the results / call her friend immediately / she
drills.target: Surprised by the results, she called her friend immediately.

acceptedAnswers: Not knowing the answer, I stayed silent.
choices: Not knowing the answer, I stayed silent.
Not knew the answer, I stayed silent.
Not knowing the answer, stayed silent I.
drills.explanation: The participle clause is formed with the -ing form after 'not'. It gives the reason for staying silent.
drills.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
drills.target: Not knowing the answer, I stayed silent.

explanation:
Adverbial participle clauses compress a time, reason, condition, or background relation into a shorter clause with an -ing form, often with a subject that is the same as the subject of the main clause. They are common in formal writing and IELTS-style sentences: 'Having finished the work, she left.' = 'After she had finished the work, she left.' The participle clause usually comes before or after the main clause, and its subject must be understood from context or be explicit in careful writing.

Be careful not to confuse this structure with a reduced relative clause. In 'The boy standing near the door is my cousin,' 'standing near the door' describes the noun 'boy'; it is not an adverbial clause. Also do not confuse it with a full time clause. 'After she finished the work, she left' and 'After finishing the work, she left' are both grammatical, but the second is the compressed participle version.

Another important point is subject control: the subject of the participle clause is normally the same as the subject of the main clause. That is why 'Driving home, I saw an accident' is correct, but 'Driving home, an accident was seen by me' sounds wrong or confusing. If the subjects are different, use a full clause instead. In formal writing, participle clauses are useful for making sentences more compact, but they must stay clear and logically connected.
explanationVi:
Mệnh đề phân từ trạng ngữ (adverbial participle clause) dùng dạng V-ing hoặc Having + V3 để nén một mệnh đề chỉ thời gian, nguyên nhân, điều kiện hoặc hoàn cảnh vào một cụm ngắn hơn. Thường chủ ngữ của cụm phân từ và chủ ngữ của mệnh đề chính là cùng một người/vật. Ví dụ: “Having finished the work, she left.” = “After she had finished the work, she left.” Đây là kiểu viết rất hay gặp trong IELTS Writing và văn phong học thuật.

Điểm dễ nhầm với người Việt là không nên nghĩ đây là mệnh đề quan hệ rút gọn. Mệnh đề quan hệ rút gọn bổ nghĩa cho danh từ, ví dụ: “The boy standing near the door is my cousin.” Ở đây “standing near the door” mô tả “the boy”, nên nó là reduced relative clause, không phải adverbial participle clause. Ngoài ra, cũng đừng nhầm với mệnh đề thời gian đầy đủ. “After she finished the work, she left” là mệnh đề hoàn chỉnh có chủ ngữ và động từ; còn “After finishing the work, she left” là phiên bản rút gọn bằng phân từ.

Lỗi rất hay gặp là dùng sai chủ ngữ. Cụm phân từ phải gắn logic với chủ ngữ của câu chính. Vì vậy “Driving home, I saw an accident” là đúng, vì chính “I” đang lái xe. Nhưng nếu chủ ngữ không khớp, câu sẽ sai hoặc gây hiểu nhầm. Khi hai chủ ngữ khác nhau, nên dùng mệnh đề đầy đủ thay vì participle clause. Trong bài IELTS, cấu trúc này giúp câu ngắn gọn và tự nhiên hơn, nhưng chỉ dùng khi quan hệ nghĩa thật sự rõ ràng.
l1Notes: Tiếng Việt thường diễn đạt quan hệ thời gian/nguyên nhân bằng các liên từ như “sau khi”, “vì”, “khi”, “trong lúc”, nên người học dễ dịch từng chữ sang tiếng Anh thay vì rút gọn bằng phân từ. Cũng hay nhầm giữa cụm phân từ trạng ngữ và mệnh đề quan hệ rút gọn vì cả hai đều có dạng ngắn. Cần nhớ: nếu cụm đó bổ nghĩa cho danh từ thì là reduced relative; nếu nó nói về thời gian/nguyên nhân/hoàn cảnh của toàn câu thì là adverbial participle clause.

minimalPairs.meaning: The participle clause shows an earlier action before the main action.
minimalPairs.sentence: Having finished the work, she left early.

minimalPairs.meaning: The full time clause expresses the same time relation in a longer, clearer way.
minimalPairs.sentence: After she had finished the work, she left early.

minimalPairs.meaning: The participle clause describes the reason or background state for the main action.
minimalPairs.sentence: Feeling tired, he went to bed early.

minimalPairs.meaning: A full time clause can express the same idea with an explicit connector.
minimalPairs.sentence: Because he felt tired, he went to bed early.
